div.head: 110 W FUNNY IT WOULD BE.
div.p: 110 W FUNNY IT WOULD BE.

(FROM BMWS ELDER BROTHER'S P013:1T OF VIEW.) If parlour chairs played hide-and-seek, Or cats were taught to purr in Greek; If Christmas Day came twice a week How funny it would be. If Lessons tasted just like sweets; Or houses ran about the street • If oysters slept ' twixt linen sheets How funny it would be. If donkeys were to crow like ct)cks, Or if the chickens ate the fox ; If seals wore Blucher boots and socks How funny it would be. If tails could wag their dogs about, Or baby's name were" Salmon Trout," Or" Half-past Six," or" Bottled Stout" How funny it would be.

If Baby cried for twenty years, And applesgrew on chandeliers' • If Ma called COCICROACEIFS "My dears," How funny it would be. And, oh! if Ma were but a plum, And Pa a green geranium, And I was only—my own thumb, How very
VRRY funny it would be. JOI. BARON.

Amateur photographer: "I've got her negative, old man." Trippode : "I thought you told irie she wouldn't sit for her picture." Amateur Photographer: "I asked her to sit with me through life, and she said 'No." A man was asked by another, with whom he was not on the best of terr..s. where he had taken up his abode. "Oh," he replied, "I'm living by the canal at present. I should be delighted if you would drop in some evening." "Are you having much practice flow?" asked an old judge of a ybuug lawyer. "Yes, sir, a good deal, thAnk you. " Ah, Pm glad to hear it. In what line is it par- ticularly ?" " Well, sir, particularly in the line of economy." Effie's brother: "Do you love my sister Effie?" Effie's steady Company: "Why, Willie, that is a queer question. Why de you want, to know?" Effie's brother: "She soh' last night she would give a sovereign to know; and I'd like to scoop it in." While a lady was feeding a hungry tramp the other day she discovered that he was pocketing her silverware. Seizing a poker, she exclaimed, "Drop those spoons, you scoundrel, and leave the ,house; leave it instantly !" "But, madame—" "Leave the house, I say; leave the house," screamed the infuriated woman. "1 go, madame," said the tramp, "never to return; but before I do I would like to say that I did not intend to take your house." There is a good story going the round of the late H enry J. Byron, which appears to have only just seen the light. When he was the manager of a Liverpool theatre, at one time he was doing especially bad busi- ness, and someone wrote to him RS follows:—" Dear Byron,—lf you are not over-crowded, can you oblige me with a box temight?" Byron replied, "Dear Boy,— Owing to a great pressure of space, I cannot let you have a box; but you can have the whole dress circle with pleasure.—Yours ever, H. J. livaox. P.S.—lf you havelany friends you would like to bring with you, you can have a few rows of stalls as well?'

Becxettnixo.—At Preston, at Matinee, at many such places, the line' go gently asunder; an fine is the angle, that at fir<t, the paths are almost parallel, and it seems of small moment whick you select. But a little further one of them turns a corner, or dives into a tunnel; and now that the speed is full, the angle opens up, and, at the rate of a mile a minute, the divided convoy flies asunder; one passenger is on the way to Italy. another to the swamps of lidlland ; one will step out in London, the other in the Irish Channel. It is not enough that you took for the better country; you must keep the way; and a small deviation may send you entirely wrong:— .r. I. Hamilton.

THR OFFICFR AND THE TIDER.—COI.Ian-Smith told an officer's adventures with a tiger, by whigh he lot an arm. He had climbed along the trunk of a tree which was slanting over a pond, and had fired at a tiger from the end of it; the tiger was wounded, but, to his horror, Captain X. saw the beast walking across the tree to- wards him. He dropned into the water, the tiger fell on him, and he was pulled ashore by the animal, who was just well enough to Neon him and munch away at the arm which he put up to protect his face. Preeent,y, the tiger, feeling very bad, retired a little way. and Captain X. had sufficient presence of mind to roll • gently back into the water, where some men came to -his rescne.—Frani Lod,/ Dufferin'n Journal. An old Scotehman„ Andrew 'Leslie, always rode a donkey to his work, and tethered him out to feed, while be laboured on the road, or wherever else he might be.. Finally, a gentleman told him that he was suspected of putting his donkey in the fields at other people's ex- pense. "Eh. laird, I could never be tempted to do that, for my cuddie winna eat anything but nettles and thistles:" One day. however, the same gentleman was riding along the road, when he saw Andrew Leslie at. work, and his donkey up to his knees in one of his own clover-fields, feeding luxuriously. ." Hallo, Andrew!" said he I thought you told me your cuddle would eat nothing but nettles and thistles." "Ay." was the reply; "but he misbeheaved the day. He nearly kicked me owe his held; sae I put him in there just to punish him."

A ROTA', POACRER.—Tra(lition asserts that Shakspere was once arrested for peachinc, and the dwellers amid the Italian Alps enjoy telling a poaching story of which their late King was the hero. As the chamois became rare, laws were made for their preservation, which were strictly entorced. One day, the king, an ardent sports- man, inadvertently shot a female chamois. A guard happened to be on the spot, Paw the animal fall, traced the shot, and not knowing that the Sportsman was the king, arrested him and led him by the arm to the nearest maeistrtrate. "What is your name and occupation?" asked the inneistrate of the accused. "Victor Emmanuel, kiln, of Raty." he quietly answered. The guard fell on his knees, the irieghtrate apologised; hut the king said to the guard: "Get up, my „good fellow, and always do your. duty. The shot of a king does as much hermits the. shot of a poacher. Only, as I think it unnecessary to take thiscese before a communal tribunal, here are five huncred francs for the fine, five hundred for my rifle, hicli you have coutiecaMd.land which I beg ynti to give me back, and live hundred for yourself. You have ;earned them." LORD DDDLETtANDIR,'BINSTITS.— The love of music is almost general in the higher spheres of English society. Amongst (then I may mention the late Lord 'Dudley. At the concerts given in his splendid house, which was almost like a garden in its wealth of flowers aneoliage plants, the leading artists were often to be heard; as was the custom at :irate concerts, they remained apart, and did not mix at all with the guests. These parties usually begin after the theatres, late at night. The fol- lowing day is lost to work; but the musicians profit by the opportunity they have of making acquaintances and receiving itivitations from house to house, and the celebrity they thus attain is more profitable to some Phan giving public concerts would be. Yet neither Madame Schumann, Joachim, nor Rubinstein considered such performances worthy of the greatness and dignity of art. I heard atil anecdote in. London about Lord Dudley and Rubinstein which illustrates; this. One day his lordship proposed that Rubinstein alwuld play for hint, and offered very high terms. The artist replied to his noble impresario. "The ticket for my concert to-day won't cost so much, my lord." Lord Dudley was not offended by the answer; he went to the concert and listened to the great pianist from a modest corner having paid several times over for his place.--4lfuerays' Magarine. CURIOUS RAILWAY INCIDEIT.—EVeryOIIe has heard of the story of the two goats which, meeting on a narrow plank bridge, butted and fought for the right ,of way. A somewhat similar incident took place a day or two ago in Brooklyn between two freight trains at a railway crossing. Traffic over the latter was delayed for over an hour by the obstinate rivalry of the two engine drivers, who, having met on the same track, would neither of them consent to reverse their locomotive, and thus make way for the other. The two engines were facing one another, and the language of the two drivers was of a nature to render the atmosphere in the vicinity redolent of brimstone. Every now and aeain they would interrupt their profanity in order to pull their levers, and attempt to force each other's train back. But the locomotives were equally matched both in power and weight, and all efforts to push one another back into the yard were doomed to failure. At length the driver of the north-bound train saw an engine coming out of the roundhouse, and which was maimed by a couple of his friends. He immediately signalled them, and they came to hie rescue by running their locomotive up to the rear of his tram. Then both engineers started up their loco- motives simultaneously. and by their combined strength the south-bound train was successfully pushed back, ' and the crossing cleared. Several thousand persons witnessed this contest of a novel and characteristically 1 American nature.

Prince George of Wales will shortly be promoted to the rank of Commander, leaping over the heads of upwards of six hundred senior lieutenants.

One result of the debate on Mr. Smith's motion will be to shut out the women's suffrage resolution. The resolution is down for Tuesday next week, and the debate on the Commission report will be pro- ceeded with de die in diem

Both the Queen and the Government regard with great satisfaction the idea of the federation of the Australian colonies. Should this scheme be carried out, it is probable that the first Viceroy of the Federated State would be a member of the Royal Family.

Miss .Olaf %rarer, an Esquimaux young lady, is tile first woman of her race who has ever come for- ward as a public lecturer. She is said to speak 1-English with great fluency, and int. Iligence, ap- pears in native costume, and only stands forty inch os high.

Prince Henry a Battenburg, if report be true,has decided to give up his small vices, such as cigarette smoking, and again unite himself to the apron strings of his Royal mother-in-law. The prince, by the/way, says a contemporary, seems to regard his mother-in-law in much the same way as mothers- in-law of the ordinary type are regarded.

The French Government are on the right track at last with the Due d'Orleans. Ile has been moved to a new pri9on, where he " can; if he chooses, learn a trade." Let it be made compulsory, and it will be the best thing the Republic • has done for many a day. If all the dukes and princes were taught trades and then made to workat them, they would give far less trouble.

A printer's error is amusing. the Queenslanders. Their leading newspaper, reviewing a work and prognosticating the wonders of science. remarked, "There need be demand no longer for Jules Verne's and other blackguards' works of imagination." The correction appeared in the !issue of the following week as follows: For other blackguards' please read Rider 1-laggard's." •

The government have accepted the invitation to the Berlin Labour Conference,and they deserve some credit for doing so. Not that their credit stands very high. If Lord Salisbury's heart had been in the cause, he would have jumped at the invitation toßerne, instead of grudgingly accepting that to Berlin. However, if the cause of labour gains, we need not look gift horses in the mouth.

A correspondent hears that Mr. Goschen is dis- posed to make a trial of the .el note system in Eng- land by giving the Bank of England power to issue a limited number of notes of that value. Specimens of the proposed paper have been engraved for the approval of the Exchequer, and Mr. Goschen will probably make reference to the matter in his Budget speecti. A special Act of ,Parliament will, of course, be needed, but the Chancellor may delay that until he sees how the public take to his scheme.

Here is the latest portrait of Louise Michel, once. well described as." the stormy petroleum of Parisian politics," painted by a compatriot :—Her face flames With color; from the centre of her ostrich-egg- shaped forehead her untidy hair cascades into her neck. She is dressed in black, and no smallest ribbon, flower, or jewel shows trace of feminine grace. She looks into vacancy. Her eyes are not fierce—filled rather with a tenderness which is the origin of all Socialism; for this woman is more Socialist by heart than by reason.'

. The. other day, in SW'. native State of Jaypore, India,' Prince Albert "Victor went a hawking with the lialuirajah's falcons. would thus take part, probably for the fist time in his life, in what was, centuries ago in our own country,the most favoured of sports. But, though the hooded hawk on fist of knight or lady has long ceased to be a familar sight in Europe, it is still common to be seen in the land where bawking wasfirst practised—in Tartary, and in Persia and native Indian States.

Regarding the eat mummies which they have been bringing in tons from Egypt to Liverpool for manure, there should be no great difficulty, accor- ding to the report, in getting tons and tons of them, again and again. Millions of mummified cats it is said, lie in the fields adjoining the remains Of the temple of Pasht or Buhastis. The cat was sacred to the goddess Pasht; and she herself had a cat's head. From far and near her worshippers brought dead cats to be embalmed and buried at her shrine.

Now that Mr. Biggar is dead. all men are saying all manner of good things about him. While be lived, and more particularly during the earlier 'por- tion of his career, no abuse was thought too coarse, no mud too foul to fling at him. Fortunately he did not care much—or, rather, be did not care at all. Re was the thickest skinned man ever 'born even in the country of O'Connell. For this I hon- our him exceedingly. After a clear head and a warm heart (and Mr. Biggar possessed both), I don't know any quality really moreestirnable than a thiek skin, Or rarer.

Mr. Wilbraham Tollemache, ivlio died last week, was the younger brother of Lord Tollemache, and fie was himself a very popular Cheshire squire, and was widely known in hunting circles as one of the finest and hardest riders that ever followed a fox. Mr. Tollemache lived at Dorf()ld Rail, a beautiful and very interesting Elizabethan manor house, which came to him, with a large estate, by his marriage with the heiress of the Rev. James Tornkinson. Mr. Tollemache has died in his eighty-third year, sin- cerely and widely regretted.

The." Star" says—"Celtus " writes to ask us to vice chapter and verse for our statement that Stanley denies being a Welshman. We don't know that there are any printed records of the matter, but it is a well-known fact that Stanley has never yet admitted his connection with Wales, although a book has been written tracing his Welsh pedigree as far as his ancestor John Rowlands. This Row- lands, by the way, was a famous man for carrying home his liquor. He was famous for his ability to sit his pony home from the alehouse, no matter what degree of intoxication he had arrived at..

Sir Edward Watkin. not content with discovering coal mines in unexpected quarters and designing towers to scale the firmament, is projecting another tunnel as a counterpart of his Channel one. • This is to connect Scotland and Ireland, and is to, run from Portpatrick in Wig,tonsbire to Lam in Antrim, the distance being less than from Dover to Calais. The intrepid nature of Sir Edward's schemes for yoking the continent cannot but excite admiration. n e have beard of a paper union with Ireland and a heart union, but Sir Edward evidently is convinced that a railway union is the only feasible solution of the Irish difficulty.

lawyers; and there seems no reason to question either the authenticity or antiquity of the unique document which Mr. Flinders Petrie has unearthed at Kahun, Or, as the town was known 4,500 years. ago, Illahnn. The document is so curiously modern in form that it might be granted probate to-day. But in any case it may be assumed that it marks one of the earliest epochs of legal history, and curiously illustrates the continuity of legal methods It consists of a settlement made by one Sekhenren in the year 44, second month of Pert, day 19—that is it is estimated the forty-fourth of Amenemhat In., or 2550 B.C.

Of the two sensational divorce cases of the spring it may be stated that no answer has yet been filed in reply to the petition presented by Captain O'Shea, the reason being that the respondentis indisposed; but there is ample time yet in which this formality can be complied with. Concerning the other, a very high-placed Anglo-Indian is now on his way nome to personally answer the allegations made by his wife. These are specially five in number, and one affects the reputation of a peeress whose name has not previously been beard of in connection with this affair, while the others include charges of a specially painful and sensational kind. Sir Charles Russell and Mr Lewis Coward will appear for the husband, and Sir Henry James will watch the inter- ests of the peeress referred to: while the Solicitor- General—it has been rumoured, but I hear without authority—is likely to be the leadingrepresentative of the petitioning wife.

Though literally wallowing in dollars, the late Mr. John Astor, the American millionaire, bore his prosperity with the utmost meekness. He was a most unpretentious man, who lived in the simplest possible manner, and worked as hard in looking after his affairs as the most zealous clerk labouring under the yoke of an inconsiderate employer. The principal heir to the great Astor fortune is Mr. Wm. Walddorf Astor, a gentleman in the prime of life, who has occupied a distinguished position in the diplomatic world as Minister of the United States to Italy, and whose reputation in Rome is that of a highly cultured and estimable American. Though men of wealth and title, from kings to baronets, have dabbled in literature, Mr. William Walddorf Astor may be possibly claimed as the first who has combined the two uncommon attributes of million- aire and novelist, for in the domain of fiction Mr. Astor has already acquired some celebrity.

Mrs. H. B. Stowe strongly belies the rumours published of her health This is said to be far better than would be inferred from the accounts that have been printed recently. Mrs. Stowe takes daily exercise, and an active interest in what is go- ing on about her. She continues her correspon- dence with her friends, and her letters—which are not, as has been said, dictated by her—show all the characteristics of the exceptionally clever letter- writer she has always been known to be. She cor- responds regularly with her friends abroad, among them the Duke of Argyll, who has just written her most appreciatively of her biography by her son, Rev. Charles E. Stowe. Mr. Gladstone, in acknow- ledging to Mr. Stowe the receipt of a copy of the `look, says : "I think it a great honour to have been selected as one of those to receive from the author copies of • The Life of Mrs. Beecher St,owe.' Mrs. Stowe has crown old amidst the adminftion of her country and of the world, and has been blessed with a period of peace in which to look • before and after.' May she reap the full fruits of that great blessing, and carry them with her, when the time arrives, into the land where it shall be per- fected."

div.head: DEATH OF " SAMMY BUTTERCUP."
div.p: DEATH OF " SAMMY BUTTERCUP."

1 The funeral of the late Mr. George Newbrooke, the original " Sammy Buttercup,' of Millhouse- brow, Croft, took place at Christ Church, Croft, on . Sunday afternoon. The deceased broke a blood vessel some months ago, and had been in failing health since, and, despite medical aid, he was con- fined to his house for several weeks, and kept grow- ing gradually weaker. He died on Thursday morn- ing week shortly after eleven o'clock. He was for many years a contributor of Lancashire sketches to the "Liverpool Weekly Post," and since he came to reside at Croft also to other papers, and also gave Lancashire readings, recitations, &c., at various entertainments in the district. His death will be much remretted by a large circle of friends in Leigh, Hindley Green, Abram. &c., where he and his wife often attended, for he wrote sketches on the prin- cipal fetes that took place there. The deceased was 54 years of age. We take the following from the "Liverpool Daily Post :"—On Sunday the mortal remains of George Newbrook, better known throughout Lancashire, and indeed the whole of the United Kingdom, as Sammy Buttercup, the author of the genial" Lan- cashire Sketches,' and "The Jubilee Debatin' Club" of the " Liverpool Weekly Post," were interred in the churchyard at Croft, near Warrington. Sammy had been ailing for a considerable time, the first symptoms of what has proved his fatal illness show- ing themselves so long ago as September last. He ' continued to grow weaker, and gradually lost the ' use of his eyesight, and became unable to read or write. He rallied somewhat towards the end of January, but catching cold early in the present month, he relapsed, and died on the 20th inst. Sammy was born in Manchester, on the sth March, 1835, and had thus almost completed his fifty-fifth year. He is survived by his widow and a grown up family. Widely known as Sammy's writings were, few could claim to liav a personal acquaint- ance with him ; ind'eed, his personality was a mystery to many. A quiet, unassuming man, one would not readily suppose that his was the hand that wrote AO many niictli-provoking tales. In the small cottage at Croft where Sammy spent the latter days of his life he composed some of his wittiest anecdotes. Brimful of that humour which pleases best of all, because it comes naturally and without any apparent effort, Saniiny's favourite couplet "Grief to our coffin adds a nail, no doubt; Whilst every grin, so merry, draws one out." expresses in small compass his own genial and love- able disposition. He was a great reader, and thought much on what he read; yet this passion for reading and writing with which he was possessed contri- buted in no small degree to his untimely death. Ile moved in a very lowly sphere of life, and thus it is that his writings will endear him In the memory of that class in particular. He Was not lacking in conversational powers, as an hour's con- versation with him would amply testify. llis mind was stored with a large amount of general know- ledge, from which be could draw to an unlimited extent. It may be of interest to note that Sammy was originally by occupation a printer. Ile resided ' for many years in Blackburn, where he published and printed his journal, known as "Dick Snow- drop's Comic Journal." Though best known by his tales and sketches, Sammy was no mean hand at the poetic art, and the verses he submitted :to the public were of more than ordinary merit. for Such. a man as Sammy Buttercup no monumental stone is required to keep his memory alive; for, though he sleeps to-darin a nameless grave, there is many a Lancashire ireside that will continue to be brigh- tened by his innocent and amusing tales.

Below we:giye a sketch by the late Lancashire writer. It is one of a series which we had pur- chased from him; and will be followed from time to time by others which he had written and which we are authorised to publish.

div.head: WARRINGTON CONSERVATIVE ASSOCIATION.
div.p: WARRINGTON CONSERVATIVE ASSOCIATION.

The annual meeting of the members of this Asso- ciation was held at the Club, Sankey-st., on Mon- day evening, Mr. John. White presiding over a good attendance. Sir Gilbert Greenell, though it ,was stated that be is much better in health; was unable to b 3 present. The Council of the Association, in their annual report, which ' was read by Alderman Sutton, and adopted on the motion of the Cl.airiaan, seconded by Mr. John Fairclough, referred With satisfaction to the general results derived from the work of the association during the past year,: and congratulated the members on its continued pros- perity. The attention and energy displayed by Mr. Ilampson in procuring the registration of all Con- servative property owners were rewarded at tilt triennial election of Guardians which tdok place in April last by a return of ten Conservative candi- dates out of twelve, the two Liberals returned being old members whom many Conservatives no doubt very properly considered it, unwise to displace. Reference was made in the report to the municipal contests; to the usual annual meetings for the C appointment. of Committees, &c. ;to the onserva- tive Club, which had recently undergone a com- plete renovation and had been beautifully decorated; : to tho series of excellent concerts held in the large Assembly Room during the winter months under the management of Mr. G. Woods; to the losses by death of many well-known and respected members of the association during the past year, namely— Mr. Beamont, Alderman Webster, Alderman John Pierpoint, Councillor Thomas Jolley, Mr. 'John Tinsley, Mr. 11. Appleton. Mr. William Bennett, Mr. James Nicholson, Mr. IL BleckleY, Mr. James Henry, &c.

div.head: THH LATH MIL mrxmonits,
div.p: THH LATH MIL mrxmonits,

The report cOirc-lt-ided. With the following reference to the late Mr. McMinnies :--" In conclusion the Council also desire to express the satisfaction they experienced in witnessing the sympathetic feeling evinced by so large a number of the Conservative party at- tending the funeral of the late Mr. J. G. McMinnies, in order to pay that last mark of respect to his memory. Although Mr. McMinnies was always an opponent in politics, there was not a Conservative who knew him who regarded him as other than a true citizen, whose excellent abilities and generous disposition, along with the persistency with which he held to his own honest con- victions, won the esteem of all classes and parties. Even the strongest political opponent must join in that true sympathy which is felt for the loss of such a fellow- townsman."

div.head: CHAIRMAN'S SPIEICH.
div.p: THE CHAIRMAN'S SPIEICH.

In the course of his speech proposing the adoption of the report,the Chairman said that the Conservative party was never in a better state of organization, or more united, and in a larger majority in Warrington than it waz at the present moment. He might also add that not within his recollection were theiropponents in a more discomfited and disorganised condition. He did not wish to glory over them; on the other hand, he would rather warn Conservatives to take a lesson from events which had happened before. They knew that history repeated itself. Twenty years ago Liberalism in Warrington was in a low condition. The Conservatives went to sleep, and what was the result ? The Liberals worked hard night after night and year after year, until at last they succeeded in returning their candidate, simply because the Conservatives had neglected their duty. When mat- ters were at the worst they began to mend, and the pro- bability was that when the Liberals had broken up their present club, and got, as it were, to the lowest rung of ladder, they would commence to re-arrange and :would bit by bit creep up ; and if the Cnnservatives were not on the look put and kept up their organizatioh they might be found napping, as PieY were in 18742 Mr. White theri proceeded to refer tO the deaths of proininent inein,bers of the ConServative party. He also paid a high compliment to the services which were being ren- dered by the Conservative Registration agent .(Mr, John Hampson), who, he paid, never left a stone unturned or allowed an opportunity to escape him ; Mr. Hampson and the association combined had done a great work for the Conservative patty of Warrington.

A COMPLIMENT TO THE " EXAMINER." Referring to the Constrvative organ, Mr. White ex- pressed regret that they had not had the assistance from the Conservative party in establishing it that they had a right to expect. A paper that was issued to reach the bulk of the working class must have an incal- cuable influence over them. The Liberals had a paper: and a good paper, too, was the" Examiner." He had not a word to say against it ; it was an excellent paper. He had no doubt the Liberals found it useful, but they (the Conservatives) could not look to it for any support to their cause. Good as the other papers might be, and useful as they might be to other parties, they were of no use to them, and he asked the Conservatives to give their support to the Conservative newspaper, because when an election came such a paper must take a great part in the contest.

SPINES seconded the resolution, which was carried, and the proceedings soon afterwards terminated.

Then there's that there nice-looking young gal as paid me once before; she'd hand it over. That's four. Ah, it's easy enough, Mr. Martin Woolford, Esquire. I can soon gat the money if you turn rusty, and say you won't pay." "If you dare to go to either of them!" cried Martin, with an evil look at the speaker. "Dare, oh! I dare r. They've paid me before, and they'll pay me again;" and the common-looking fellow is light trousers and cut-away coat, with spotted handkerchief, and a great pin of gilt brass made to represent a saddle with stirrups and bridle, pulled down his cuffs and arranged his collar as if he were going off at once. "Now look here, Dick Worrell," cried Martin Woolford; "I've told you, and I tell you again, pay you." "Then why clon'tcher do it?" said the man. 'lf you can't pay your debts, why don'teher leave oi! betting amongst gentlemen as can? You're getting :13 had as a welsher.' , "You came and asked fur sue at the office this after- noon." "Of course I did. / came for my monev—TrY money, do you hear? I didn't come for your money, I same for my money as I won lawful, and which you wouldn't pay.' "It's likely to do me great injury if you come them, Dick, and I won't have it." " Won'tcher?" said the man; "then pay me my con. temptible thirty pun as is Puch a little dirty bit ti money to big Mr. Martin Woolford, Esquire," he con- tinued, with contemptible galling iteration. "I'll pay you this day fortnight," said Martin at last, Hs he turned down out of the strand, eo as to be in a less public place. "You're agoing to pay me now," said the fellow with a hoarse laugh. " You've put me off till I wou'i be put off no longer, and I just tell you what, I'm ei, her going to knock it out of the people I've mullet or else I'm going to stick by you till you hand over; and just you tete my advice—don't you get besting again it you haven't got the money to stand the racket.'

_ Martin Woolford's fists involuntarily clenched than- selves, and he seemed for the moment as if be were going to strike the man, as they reached the com- paratively deserted Embanktuent ; but the fellow srivr it, and threw himself into an attitude of defence.
" Oh, that's it, is it P" he saici, cisrming and feintint from one side to the other, ducking his heed, and making helieve to inflict savage Mows. " ready; rome_on then."

"Don't bee fool, Dick," cried Martin. impatiently. "Why not you be reasonable?" "I'll be reasonable enough when you pay me what you Owe me "IT pay it when lye got it," said Martin, sulkily. "Now :Viii (:)11 M;N eoodnees to go, sir?' " 013,10r'.' said the an, insolently " we're to go, are we. I allera ,hutight. the 'bankluent was as free for one party as it was for another. I don't know as I sin% right, so I shall stop here till I get my thirty pound." Martin looked at him in a fashion that indicamd wt.at would have been the fate of Mr.nichard Woeralt. betting man, well known in the various sporting ullit;es about Fleet-street, had Martin Woolf°, d been some eattern chief or king. But as he we only a clerk on a very precarious tenurt in the firm of Humphreys and Company, West India merelkants, he walked sharply off along the pavement, and look-'i!over the low wall at the river, which seemed to be all aolaze with His reflections of the various lamp.

At the end of ten minutes Le began to be hopeful that Worrell had given up in diegu4t, and left boo; but to his horror there was the fellow close botanic' taking step for step, and following him with the per• tinacity of a shadow. What should he do? What could he do? The man bad said that he would apply to one or the other of his friends, and they had paid money for him so frequently that he looked upon such an application with horror. • He called himself fool—au— idiot, and then lamented his Want of luck. Here was this low- bred ruffian, who bad not a tittle of his education and polish, let alone his addreis, stwessful again and again over his betting transactions, while he, Martin Weol • ford, never seemed to succeed. That last venture had seemed so certain; and if he had won ha would have been three hundred and fifty pounds in pocket, and could have paid off several awkward debts. But then he had not won, and the consequence was that this fellow and several others of his stamp would be hunting him until be had paid them, and tho only way to do it seemed to be to make Aber ventures, even if they were reckless, so as to win ths money that would set him free. . He walked on and on fuming and fretting. cursing ,

hi a very existence, and asking himself how the river could flow on so calmly while he was in such weariness of spirit. Suppose he appealed to Mark once more. No; he dare not do it. Suppose he asked his mother to help him. She would, he knew, but she had not the money. Her watch, chain, and some treasured trinkets were even now in pledge, placed there by him to pay off a betting debt. No; it was useless to go to her. Ruth? Yes; why not go to gentle, pretty little Ruth? He had but to plead to her, and tell her what trouble he was in to gam her sympathy, and she would let him have the money. But it was impossible. He knew she would not have it on hand, though she had a little dowry of her own. I must get rit:Lof him by promises," he muttered, as they were getting towards Westminster, every step being in a contrary directioa to that in which he wished to go. Mr. Richard Worrell. knew his well enough, for he said suddenly: "Now then, grainer, isn't it time we turned 111) north?" "Look here," said Martin, turning upon him. and walking in the other direction, "what do you want me to do?" "Pay up." "But I have told you that I have no money." "Then you must get it, for I ain't going to be pull off any longer. I wouldn't mind waiting if it was only ' myself, but there's a chap I know as stood in halves ' with me. and I daren't go back without the ca.h." " Liar l" said Martin to himself. "low ana r get it ?" he said, aloud. "How are you to get it?" said the fellow, with a sneer. "How would any ?hap get it as te situated like you? Why, he'd borrow it from the firm for aI ew days, and pay it back as soon as he could, and not keen- gents as he had engagements with waiting for the,r money." "Borrow from the firm," cried Martin, contemP- tuously. "If you had any brains you would know that it's impossible. They would not let me have sovereign to save my life." "Then I shouldn'ttell 'em I wanted it, but I shoila borrow it all the same."

" What ! steal it?" cried Martin, indignantly. " Steal ? Why what a flat you are, Woolfordr Wouldn't you pay it back as soon as you could? lloW could that he stealing?" Martin Woolford stopped near one of the flights of river steps, and leaning his arms on the low wall stood gazing over at the water. "Well, why don'tcher speak? Can't you hear ? " "Yes, I hear plainly enough." "Well then, look here, my lad, if you'll agree to bring me that money to-morrow night at this time, let you off till then.' " I can't bring you the money," said Martine coldly. "But you've got to bring it, I tell you," said the man,. tauntingly. "Why, if I liked to speak out I could bring a dozen fellows to Duggan - len& to-morrow morning to see me righted, and they wouldn't go away, not one of 'ern, till they had seen it done. Dyer bear? till they had seen it done, and tsi soy, spent on 'ern in drink besides." Martin Woolford shivered at the idea of the :Nei quiet offices being invested by such a ruff. tidy rrex would be Mr. Dick Worrall's companions, al.cl At be same time he felt no doubt that the frillier i to some extent, carry out his threats—such, fr i•esatice. as coming to the place as he had done that eas, sending in for him before proceeding to mon imaged action. In imagination, as he stood there leaning On the wall, he saw the low-lived party standing in the lea low room appropriated to the clerks, and sew his brother's stern, reproschful face iipbreiding for bringing such disgrace upon him. Ile pictured. old Mr. Klopstock, the manager, bidding loin some' into his private room previous to reportiti„s his son- duct to the principals, and be could almost have repeated what the old man would say. He recalled, too, his many offeness a‘raimtt the regularity of the plasm, and the warnises hrel He knew that another lapse or two would rieult 'n an ignominious discharge, and that he bad been regularly saved again and again by his brother. "No," he argued, " this fellow must he prfoiyo,ed from coining at any cost. I must do soinethisg, but what?" Martin Woolford was growing desperate, and his self-constituted companion impatient. "Now lookye here," he exclaimed. "What's the good o' you cutting up rough. You've got to ens its you know." "How could he have been such an idiot as Si) rise himself in this man's power," Martin asked and the inconvenience it caused hiin made him for the time being feel somethieg like bitter repenmace, but he made no reply. "If you'll be civil, I don't mind putting you up to a dodge or two that would be useful to a chap like 'oil." " A dodge or two!"—in other words give him a hint how he might ron his employers. Martin Woolford felt this, and, with a gesture of disgust, he walked on for a short distance and paused as his aompanion walked close up alongside. "I'd run if I was you, Mr. Martin Woolford ; but you'd have to run precious fast to get away from me. More obstinate you gets, more obstinate I gets. I risaY as well tell you at once that I got on and made money by being obstinete and sticking to fellows till they Paid - up. I've had to do with lota of such gents as you. as would take to betting and backing horses; and they've tried to get out of their engagements, same as 7011'r8 doing." "I tell you lam not," cried Martin, fiercely. a I want is time." "Yes, so you said last week; so you said weak afore; and so you said week afore that. Every ail this month I've had to dun you for that bit o' money. It's disgusting, that's what it is, Mr. Merlin Viroolford, it's disgusting. You're a defaulter, that's what wi are, and all the time you're pretending to be a gent. ~,, • But it won't do, you know. I've had to deal wen worse ones than you, and I've always got my nensel• What did you go backing horses for ? " "AL, why indeed!" groaned Martin, as he thought of the misery it had caused him. "You ain't honest, that's what you ain't," said the fellow; "and when I has a chap to deal with as sin t honest. I knows how to deal with him." The Embankment was pretty well deserted as they stood there. Now and then a cab trundled by over the level road, and at times a pedestrian passed them: but their coming was rare, and more than oare Murray felt a desperate kind of thought as to how he might escape for the moment from the fellow? importunity. He was pretty active, and a quick pulp would send him off the edge of the unprotected stairs into the muddy stream, wh re he might struggle Out as he could, and such a bold attack might CO the fellow into submissiveness, But no; that would not do. It would be mad tO attempt such a thine. The fellow might be sweg away and drowned; and a shudder rens through t young man as he thought that such an act would he murder. His thoughts were wandering off the next moment, and he asked himself whether it would not be better to shakeoff the scoundrel for the moment by trusting to his own swiftness of flight. Worrell might perhaps shout "Stop thief," but there were so few people about that the chances were that he might get away, and after all it would be better to make confession to his brother and trust to him to help him to set the felloW at defiance than to remain as it were under his thumb. "You're not honest," repeated Worrell just then, in an aggravating key; " d'yer hear, I say you are not honest." "Should I be honest if I robbed or embezzled to pay you?" cried Martin, turning upon him so &soar that the man receded a few steps. • g,?l "Who wants you to do either o' be said, as Martin walked right to the edge of t r stone pier. "I says borrow the money of /V_ people, and pay it again when them ugly nsthin ne you've bad see ts's pickings. And, look here, if you'll pay me," he added in a whisper, "and will provide yerself with a fifty, o,e_ so, I'll put iyou up to a good thing or two —o,lt-., out good things—where you'll be safe to win, and t efl —. No you don't, my lad! you'd run, would you!" • For, just as he was uttering his temptation—sticih one as has assailed many a young men before now Martin made a spring to dash off imud run. But Visorrall was too quick for him, and, closing. held him tightly by the arms. "Loose me, you blackgu,ird," cried I/ fiercy: "How dare you touch me!" And, desperate. strung up to a pitch of fury by his compel-I clever way of baffling, his intended flight, be turned.r upon him savagely. They wrestled for a moment two—nearer and nearer the edit'; one of them mane a false step—there was a hoarse cry, a sudden pluade, and the muddy tide swept nest' their heads. (To be oorstiatz.l-1.)

DEPERIAL PARLIAMENT. .
HOUSE OF LORDS.-MONDAY.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four ( 'clock.) PRIVATE BILLS, B,:c.—The Widnes Brine Supply Bill was read a second time.—The Bootle-cum-Linacre Cor- poration Bill, the Liverpool Corporation Bill, thf, Ribblo Navigation Bill, and the Wallasey Local Board Bill were read a second time.—A Bill introduced by LorA Herschel' for enabling incorporated companies to act as executors and in other fiduciary capacities was read a second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Law.—Lord Lamington (the Hon. C. W. Baillie Cochrane) took the oath on succeeding to the title. The House adjourned at ten minutes to five o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.-14IoNDAy. . . .

The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. THE PARNELL COMMISSION REPORT.—Mr. J. MORLEY. I on behalf of Mr. Gladstone, gave notice of an amend- ment to the Government motion on the subject of the report of the Special Commission. The amendment ex- presses in strong terms the repudiation by the House of the false charges made against some of its members, satisfaction at the exposure of the calumnies, and regiet for the wrong inflicted and the suffering and loss en- dured " by reason of this gross and flagrant iniquity." Sir C. LEWIS intimated that in the event of the amend- ment being carried he would move an addition deplor- ing that by the report it was found that nine members of the House were parties to a treasonable conspiracy, and that 43 members were parties to a criminal con- spiracy, and expressing the opinion that the conduct of such members was deserving of severe condemnation. NEW WRITS.—New writs were ordered to fill vacancies in the representation of North St. Pancras and the Stam- ford Division of Lincolnshire. THE SALFORD GAS SCANDAL.—The HOME SECRETARY could not at present inform Mr. Howard what action, if any, was necessary on the part of the Government with reference to the Salford gas scandal. HALFPENNY POSTCARDS.—Mr. W. L. JACKSON informed Mr. Heaton that if postcards were sold for a halfpenny each, instead of at the present rate, there would be a loss to the Treasury of £31,000 per annum. THE CLONGOREY EVICTIONS.

Mr. SEXTON having obtained the necessary support moved the adjournment of the House in order to call attention to" the illegal and violent coupe of conduct" of the police at Clongorey, in endeavouring to prevent the erection of huts for some evicted tenants. He des- cribed at length the proceedings at Clongorey, and de- nounced the putting into force the Act of Edward 111. against a parish priest and the workmen who were build- ing huts for the homeless and houseless people. Mr. BALFottn, in reply to Mr. Sexton, pointed out in- accuracies and exaggerations in his speech, amid inter- ruption on the part of Mr. Sexton; justified the action of the police and magistrates, and told the House that by voting for the adjournment they would he voting in favour of the defiance of the law by people bn cked by a powerful conspiracy, and would be striking the greatest blow conceivable at the prosperity of Ireland. After a brief debate, in which Sir C. Russell and the Attorney- General for Ireland took part, the motion for the adjournment was defeated by 196 votes to 154.

THE DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS. Mr. A. THOMAS resumed the debate on the Address by moving an amendment in favour of the establishment Of an independent department of the State for the conduct of distinctly Welsh affairs, presided over by a Mmister acquainted with the national characteristics of Wales. This was seconded by Mr. Pritchard Morgan, but opposed by the Hon. George Kenyon, Mr. Osborne Mor- gan (who held that it was opposed to the Welsh Home Rule movement), and by the Home Secretary, after which it was withdrawn. Mr. GRAHAM then moved an amendment calling atten- tion to the increasing desire of the working-classes in Europe for legislative restriction of the hours of labour, which rendered it desirable that the subject should be discussed by the representatives of this country who should be appointed to attend the international labour conference at Berne or Berlin. The amendment was rejected by a large majority. The Address was then agreed to amid cheers. NEW Blus.—Sir Wm. Houldsworth brought in a Bill for the amendment of the Companies Act, 1862, and Sir Albert Rollit a Bill to amend the law relating to trustee savings banks, and one to amend the law as to deeds of arrangements'. These were read a first time, and the House adjourned at 20 minutes past twelve, HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. _ . .

The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. THE Lanolin CONFERENCE.—Sir J. FERGIISSON an- nounced that the Government had expressed their wil- lingness to take-part In the labour conference proposed by the German Emperor. Os POUND NOTES.—Mr. Gescdsw said he was not aware of any Bill intended to give barks the privilege of issuing £1 notes. BRIBERY BY CoNntecroas.—Lord GEORGE HAMILTON intimated that he had directed Bell's Asbestos Company, Limited, to be informed that at the expiration of their present contract their names would be removed from the list of contractors to the Admiralty. THE VAN AND WHEEL TAX.—MT. GrOSCHEN, replying to Mr. J. Bryn Roberts, said he had received a lame number of memorials in favour of the van and wheel' tax, but they did not deal with the important question as to the licence duty proposed for pleasure horses. It was not for him to reintroduce the measure ;it was for the president of the Local Government Board to discovert local taxes, and to be the hero or the victim of the next tax that might be proposed. CIVIL SERVICE ESTIMATES. g The House afterwards went into committee on the Civil Service and Revenue departments supplementary estimates. Several votes were obtained, the chief dis- cussions bearing on the work of the newly-created Board of Agriculture and of the Maritime Conference recently held at Washington. 'On a supplementary vote of £23.250 for charges con- nected with Bechuanaland and other services in South Africa, Sir GEORGE CAMPBELL moved to reduce the vote by I £20,009 for police in Bechuanaland. He thought such a charge was one which the new chartered company should bear. Baron HENRY DI WORMS stated that the police were , for the purpose of preventing filibustering on frontiers of our territory. - Mr. LABOUCHERB said the Government had made a present of four millions sterling to the company. • After some further discussion the amendineni Was negatived lay 143 to 79. , The Committee next discussed briefly the question of Swaziland, but the Government declared its inability at present to state what course they would adopt in refer- ence to that country, as they had not considered Sir Francis de Winton's report. Some further votes were agreed to. and progress was reported at midnight. The House adjourned at 12.15 pm. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four o'clock. Miscxtzawzons.—A bill presented by Lord Knutsford to amend the law in regard to the adminstration of Admiralty jurisdiction in her Majesty's dominions out- side the United Kingdom, was read a first time. On the motion of the BISHOP of CARLISLE, the Cathedral Churches Bill was read a second time, is object being to provide for making statutes respecting cathedral chapters in England, and for others purposes relating thereto. The EARL of HARROWBY asked whether the Government were prepared to fulfil their engagements to the County Councils of England and ° Wales, in order that they might receive without further delay the additional sum of not less than £700,000 per anzum in relief of local rates, which was promised to the ratepayers. Lord Cranbrook replied that there was no engagement as to the special sum to be provided, or as to the special means to he adopted, except that the money was to come from local sources. Lord Rirox said that if the Government did not do something to satisfy the just expectations of the County Councils they must be prepared to be troubled with a loud outcry from many important public bodies against the course they were pursuing. Lord Basing and Earl Fortescue expressed the same views, and the subject dropped. Their lordships rose at twenty-five minutes to six o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS, .YVEIMESDAT.

The Speaker took the chair at half-past twelve. QUESTIONS, &C.-Mr. BAISOUR, replying to Mr. Carew and Mr. Sexton, justified the action of the police in refer- ence to the Clongorey evictions. Mr Labouchere, having ascertained from the Financial Secretary to the Treasury that it was intended to take the vote on account to- morrow, gave: notice to call attention to a gross scandal in matters relating to the administration or justice in England. IRISH POOR LAW BILL.-Mr, P. J. FOLEY moved the 'second reading of the Poor Law Guardians (Ireland) Bill, which, he explained, was substantially a reproduc- tion , of former bills. Mr. J. O'CoNnon seconded the motion, and Colonel WARING mo'ved that the bill he read a second time that day six months. Mr. Balfour said he was prepasKl to assent to the second reading of the bill, but intimated that he would do his best in Committee to remove those pro- visions which he thought would not conduce to the due administration of the poor 14w in Ireland or to the benefit of all classes of the community. Colonel Waring wi hdrew his amendment,and the second reading was agreed to; but on the motion of Mr. Sexton it was agreed that Com- mittee on the Bill be taken that day six months, the measure being consequently shelved. The County Coun- cils Association (Expenses) Bill was read a second time. 'Mr. Burt brought in a Bill to provide for the regulation of vans, vehicles, and tents used as dwellings. COMPENSATION FOR UNJUSTIFIABLE PRO.ECUTION.-011 the motion fer the adjournment of the House, Mr. SEX- TON informed the Attorney-General for Ireland that the Court of Queen's Bench had that day quashed the con- viction of Mr. Henry O'Connor, sub-editor of the " Leinster Leader," who has been sentenced to two months' imprisonment (Nationalist cheers) and marked its special sense of the conduct of the magii- trates who convicted Mr. O'Connor, by ordering process against them. (Renewed cheers.) He wanted to know whether the Government would consider the question of compensating Mr. O'Connor, and would exercise parti- cular supervision over the magistrates who dealt with

his case. The ATTORNEY-GENERAL for lrelana said the questions raised were serious ones, and he must have notice of them. The House adjourned at five minutes to Sir. HOUSE OF LORDS.—Tmmsnny. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at a quarter-past four o'clock. THF. LAW OF PARTNERSHIP.—The LORD CHANCELLOR moved the second reading of a bill trg declare and amend the law of partnership. The bill, he said, defined the nature of partnership, settled the legal status of partners and the relations between partners themselves, and then dealt with the dissolution of partnership and the conse- quence which followed.—Lord HERSCHELL cordially welcomed the measure. The bill was read a second time, and the House adjourned at twenty-five minutes to five. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TntrasnAv.

The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. Qn&Thous &c.—Questions were asked relative to the hours of factory workers in India, the Behring Sea dis- pute, and affairs in Crete. In reply to Mr. Bryce, Sir J. FERGUSSON on the latter point said that the Government had no information of any intention on the part of the Porte to modify the recent Firman ; still he held that the state of the country was more hopeful. The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER in reply to Sir R. Paget, said as soon as there was the slightest chance of carrying the van and wheel tax he should have pleasure in reviving the proposal. WESTERN AUSTRALIA.—Baron H. nu Woums moved the second reading of the Western Australia Constitution Bill, which sanctioned an Act of the Legislature of West em Australia- giving responsible government to that colony. Sir G. CAMPBELL had given notice of an amend- ment, but he did not move it, declaring, however, that the fullest discussion should take place before Parliament consented to hand over to a handful of colonists the only remaining temperate lands in our possession. In the debate which followed the speakers included Mr. Osborne Morgan. Sir G. Baden-Powell, Mr. Seton-Karr, Mr. Sydney Gedge, Mr. Chamberlain, and Mr. S. Smith. The hon. member for Flintshire was unable to support the proposal that the land of Western Australia should be given to the present occupiers, who had done all in their power to discourage British emigration. The Bill was read a second time and referred to a Select Com- mittee. MISCALLANEOUS.—The Companies (Winding-up) Bill and the Companies (Memorandum of Association) Bill were mid a second time. Mr. E. Stanhope, dealing with the question of barrack accommodation, said he had inspected the cavalry barrack in Manchester and was satisfied that it should not be maintained. The House adjourned at ten minutes past twelve o'clock.

Rowe returned the leek off, but a fast Westmoreland, two or three week, a.fo. 'nit. ga Me follow up by Oldham shortly afterwards considerably was played at Whitt-haven IITI.I the visitors 41141 all the I improved their position, but a minor was given after ,coring, tries being Obtair.e4l Ir. I,:olhanzh. Kent, auti a Speakman running to the line. When half-time arrived goal from midfield by 1'a441. Pao! al-w .lazvorte..: (n,.. of Warrington led by 3-1-2 to nil. Changing ends and re- I the tries. Cumberland were only conceded one Minor. ' starting, Oldham at once dribbled splendidly, and I Obliged the home team to touch down. McDonnell finely returned the drop, and some determined play by the visitors put the Warringtonians on their mettle. Eventually Mather threw to Jolley, who brought relief by a huge punt, and Davies by a strong run further im- proved the position. Some good forward play by Wolestenholme, Beaver, and, Lees found the home team again defending, until the home front van, led by Catterall, Johnson, and Russell, broke away. This was further enhanced by a capital dribble by Jolley, Sowden, saving daringly on the line. The ball was got out of danger by Lees, the home forwards about this time play- ing somewhat loosely. From a subsequent scrimmage Rowe almost dropped a goal, a minor accruing. 1 Oldham now rushed to midfield, and after Webster had stopped a rush, Russell threw across to Speakman. Give-and-take play ensued, Thornley in the meantime dribbling well into the opponent's quarters, where Davies and Alolyneux strove hard to get over. By intercepting some passes Oldham were enabled to clear, and subse- quently dribbled to the opposite end of the field, where Buckley saved a try. Shortly afterwards Beaver, for the visitors, got a try, which Tulloy improved. The home team now wakened up, and rushed away to their oppon- ents' quarters, where Holmes, Catterall, and Isherwood dribbled to the line, and from a screw scrimmage Neild got a good try. Buckley next showed up with a strong run to the line, and Jolley taking the ball splendidly, almost got over, but directly afterwards Webster, who was lying well up, dropped a remarkably ,fine goal from the midst of his opponents. Restarting, Oldham, by charging a kick, took the game to Warrington quarters, Mather finally getting the oval away, and from a long kick by Jolley, another minor was conceded. Nothing more was scored and Warrington' ran out winners by 42-4 to 1-0-1. Teams—Wamngton : Webster, back; Buckley, Jolley, and Speakman, three-quarters; Mather and Rowe, half backs; Isherwood, Neild, Molyneux, Davies, Russell, Johnson, Catterall, Holmes, and Thorn- ley, forwards. Oldham: Sowden : back; McConnell, Cowley, and Hilton, three-quarters; Bentley and Nolan, half backs; Ripley, Lees, Whittaker, Tuhoy, Wolsten- holme, Randle, Murrell, Kershaw, and Beaver, for- wards.

FOOTBALL —ASSOCI N. Mr. Horne, of Accrington. had a lively experience 0' the disagreeable side of football refereeing on Saturday. He was referee in the league match between the Black- burn Rovers and Burnley, at Burnley, and an impression seemed to get abroad that lie was biased against the home team because his brother was the Rovers' goal- keeper. When a second goal by Burnley was disallowed the hooting lasted several minutes, and when he allowed the Rovers' last point the home players refused for five minutes to proceed with the game, the spectators all the while urging them to leave the field. At the close of the game the police were unable to keep the ground clear, and thousands rushed towards the referee, who had an anxious time of it for half an hour. He was at length taken to a house and afterwards driven away in a cab under the protection of the police, bat the crowd fol- lowed and hooted him.

....... RUNCORN " A " TEAM V. WILMSLOW.—At Runcorn, on Saturday, and after a very one-sided game, the home team retired the victors by 4 goals, 3 tries, to nil. WARRINGTON V. OLDHAM.— The Warrinonians journeyed to Oldham on Saturday to play off their re- turn fixture, but on arrival at that place the fog was found to be so densethat play, was imposzable, and the match was accordingly abandoned. WARRINGTON 2ND V. CHESTER COLLEGE.—ThiS match was played at Chester, on Saturday. The Warriegtonians commenced the game, and at once attacked in vigorous style. The first to open the scoring account was Lally, who was followed by Williams, Knowles, and Barnes. Lally again scored after a fine run. Newton placed the goals. Battersby played a fine game for the Cestrians. Final score: Warrington, two goals, four tries, three minors ; Chester, two minors. WIDNES v. ROCHDALE ST. Cramerrs.—The Rochdale St. Clement's team visited Widnes on Saturday, where a most stubborn contest with the representatives of the chemical centre ended in a draw of one minor each. Barton, for St. Clement's, got hurt early on, and was of little use afterwards. The visiting forwards showed up well, and on one occasion Oddy got over the line after a grand dribble, but the point was disallowed. L. Rigg, Thompson,and M. Heywood behind, and Waugh, Dex, and Oddy forwards, were most conspicuous for St. Clement's, whilst Parkinson, Plumpton, and Farrell played finely for Widnes. RUNCORN V. HUDDRRSPIELD.—One of the grandest games seen on the Huddersfield ground for • some time resulted from the return encounter between Runcorn and Huddersfield. Neither side was able to place its full strength on the field, for in addition to the the playing in the " big" match at Bradford, Kingston, Hancock. Gaytor (Runcorn). T. H. England, Haigh, and Jackson (Huddersfield) were absent from their respective sides. Play was of the fastest and most interesting character. imaginable. The passing of the visitors was indeed a treat to witness, but the way in which the home forwards played in the loose, and the fine tackling of their backs, more than neutralised any advantage which the wearers of the dark green might otherwise have gained. In the first half Huddersfield played up hill,and quickly initiated the scoring as the result of a prettily-dropped goal from the foot of Fred Richmond. The visitors, however, were not to be denied, and from a good try gained byFaulkner Brazendale was able to equalise. On changing ends, Huddersfield had all the best of the play, Charlie Sykes scoring two tries and Fred Kaye and Frank Walker one each, and upon two of them Richmond (who took all the kicks at goal) was able to improve. Runcorn played the pluckiest game of any team seen at Fartown for a long time, and kept their opponents ever on the alert until the referee's whistle closed an interesting game with the score—Huddersfield, three goals, two tries, and three Itninors ; Runcorn one oat and two minors. The game was not so one-aided as the score would indicate, the play throughout being very exciting. . WARRINGTON A. V. OLDHAM A.—Splendid weather favoured this return fixture, which was played at War- rington on Saturday, before a numerous assemblage oi spectators. The home team was somewhat weakened through vacancies in the premier fifteen having to be filled ; the Oldhamites, on the other hand, mustering strongly, anticipating a victory, but their expectations in this case were not realized, the Warringtomans ex- celling in every department, especially in the passing. Throueh the late arrival of the visitors it was half-past four orclock when Isherwood started, and a fine screw kick by Jolley soon put the visiting team on the defence, Buckley almost getting over after a bit of passing by the home half backs, and a minor was conceded to avert disaster. The drop qut was well returned, but Cowley got the oval out of danger, and enabled his side to gain a footing at midfield. After a spell of pretty passing be- tween Rowe, Mather and Jolley a splendid dodgy run by Speakman enabled that player to gain a try, which Webster failed to improve. By the aid of the drop out ' the visitors gained a temporary footing at centre, where Holmes threw wide to Speakman, who, unfortunately stumbled, and a smart cress dribble by Beaver, Tuhoy, and Ripley, supplemented by Cowley dashing through his opponents, completely reversed matters • but Buckley coming across from the opposite wing, stopped the im- pending danger at the home quarter flag. The home team, who were now showing rare combination and beautiful passing, gave the visitors an anxious time of it, and after Nolan had stopped an impetuous rush by Molyneux, Isherwood, and Davies, a capital spell of pass ing by Rowe, Mather, and Jolley, who threw finely across to Buckley, almost resulted in a try. Strive how they would, the Oldham team could not keep out the Warringtomans, but after Speakman had had a splendid try disallowed, Thornley gained one immediately after- wards, which Webster converted. Thornley foiled the kickoff, and Webster, who, up to now, had been idle, put in a grand piece of work, transferring play from his own quarters to the Oldham 25. Oldham, however, led by Ripley and Bentley, put in a grand cross dribble, !Nut this was more than neutralized by a display of pass- ing between Mather Jolley, Catterall, Molyneaux and Rowe, which resulted in the latter dashing over the line, Webster kicking a goal. The following team has been selected to'represent Eng- land in the match to-day with Scotland at Edinburgh : W. G. Mitchell (Richmond), back; A. R. Stoddart (Black- heath), P. H. Morrison (Cambridge), and J. Dyson (Hud- dersfield), three-quarter backs; F. H. Fox (Somerset- shire), and F. Bonsor (Bradford), half-backs; D. Jowett (Heckmondwike), H. Bedford (Morley), L. Hickson and .1. Toothill (Bradford), E. Holmes (Manningham), S. M. J. Woods (Cambridge), A. Robinson (Blackheath), F. Evershed (Burton), and A. Rogers (Moseley), forwards.

Crompton, the Runcorn centre three-quarter distin- guished himself in the match Yorkshire v. The Rest of England, at Bradford, on Saturday, and in fact he was the only player who scored for his side. The Yorkshire- men upheld their reputation by defeatiag the " Rest of England" by one goal three tries to one goal one try and one minor, the neatly dropped goal and the try of the defeated team being due to Crompton.

To-day's matches :—Warrington v. -Free Wanderers, away; Runcorn v. Birkenhead Park, at Runcorn; Wid- nes v. Leigh (League 'natch), at Leigh; St. Helens v. Wigan (League match), at Wigan; St. Helens Recs. v. Kendal Hornets at Kendal.

Runcorn journeyed to Huddersfield on Saturday with a very weak team, indeed at one time there was a doubt if they could raise a team at all, and paid the penalty by a rather severe defeat. In palliation it may be stated that the ground was little better than a quagmire, and the home players broke the oft-side rule without com- punction much to the detriment of the visitors. This is only the secon,cl defgat Runcorn have received in the home and fume fixtures.

The regretof the Runcornians at the dc feat was more than compensated for by the brilliant display of Cromp- ton for England against Yorkshire. There is a wonder- ful concensus of opinion amongst the scribes that he si as the best back on the field, and his running, kicking, and passing are the subject of general remark. He scored a try after a sprint half the length of the field, through tile Yorkshire pack, and dropped a goal; the only tangible points made by England. After this performance it was thought that he could not be passed over for the match England Scotland, on Saturday, hut he had to give way to older if not better players. He is, however, first reserve three-quarter, and as it is very unlikely that Stoddart will be equal to fulfilling his engagement, Crompton will most probably have to do duty in his stead.

After his success on Saturday, Crompton was con- gratulated by Mr. Rowland Hill, secretary of the Union, and other " big guns," and the former g,entlemr n pre- sented him with his international jersey and said he was sorry he could not give him his cap. As Crompton is only 19 years of age, he is likely. with ordinary luck, to have his name "writ large' in the annals of foot- ball.

div.p: NISCRLLANROITS.

Liverpool met Aberdeen in the second round of the competition for the National Physical Recreation Society's challenge shield, at Aberdeen, on Saturday. For bar- bells, the two teams were adjudged equal, each being awarded the maximum of 98 points. For parallel bars, however, the Liverpool eight obtained 79, and the Aber- deen men 694. At high Jump Aberdeen came to the front with 85 marks, while Liverpool had 81. At this stage Lrverpool were thus leading by 64 marks, and they increased this advantage in rope climbing, obtain- ing 601 marks to 574 for Aberdeen. The totals were : Liverpool, 3294; Aberdeen, 311; majority for Liverpool, 94 points. For the first time in four years Aberdeen is thus put out of the final. It ought to be stated that in the North great dissatisfaction is felt at the judging in the barbell and .parallel epar exercises, and a protest is probable. The Judges wbre Mr. Thomas, Liverpool, and Captain Downman, Gordon Highlanders, the referee being Colonel lanes, R.A., of Learney.
As I have before mentioned Warrington will to-day meet Bournemouth in the competition in the Circus, Warrington.

div.head: LANEROH DISASTER.
div.p: THE LANEROH DISASTER.

1 The coroner's inquiry into the Lanerch Colliery disaster was resumed at Pontypool, on Wednesday, when the re- examination of Ashman, the fireman, was proceeded with. He stated that he made a complete inspection of the workings, and was of opinion that naked lights might be used with safety. He had found small quantities of gas, but nothing that he thought it necessary to report. The jury, however, expressed the opinion that all accu- mulations of gas, whether great or small should be re- ported. The inquiry was adjourned. The inquest on the men killed in the disastrous explo. sion at Llanerch Colliery was resumed on Thursday. One of the witnesses stated that the men had never been asked to use safety lamps, and the only reason why naked lights were preferred was one of wages. Several miners said that they had at various times found gas in the pit but had not reported it. The inquiry was again adjourned.

div.head: LABOUR AND CAPITAL.
div.p: LABOUR AND CAPITAL.
The West Yorkshire miners on Wednesday gave in notices for a 10 per cent, advance, and it is understaod that 5,000 notices will have been handed in from Yorkshire. _

' The miners at Normanton, Sharleston, Stanley, All- tofts, Methlev, Featherstone, Pontefract, and Woodles- ford, West Yorkshire, on Thursday gave in notices for a 10 per cent. advance. A Berlin telegram of Wednesday states that the Powers have signified their adhesion to the Emperor William's proposal for an International Labour Congress. It is understood that the conference will assemble on March 15th. It is announced that the programme of the International Conference on Labour is restricted to questions affecting Sunday labour and the labour of women and children. The French Cabinet yesterday accepted" in principle "..the invitation to take part in the Conference. IMPENDING GREAT MINERS' STRIKE.

A strike -tiffecting.lo,ooo hands is threatened on the part of the miners In Nottinghamshire. Endorsing the decision arrived at recently at the National Conference in London, the men have decided to give in notice for a 10 per cent increase. The notices are to expire in the second week in March, when, unless the advance is con- ceded, the men will come out. RAILWAY WORKMEN'S AGITATION. _ _

The men employed in the Furness Railway Company's works at Barrow recently petitioned the directors to give them back the 5 per cent, which was deducted from their wages nearly three years ago, during the worst time of the depression. The locomotive superintendent has informed the men that the directors have declined to give any advance of wages at present. Thi. decision has been received with very great dissatisfaction and the men threaten to strike unless the advance is forth coming.

div.head: TIM JUDGES' REPORT.
div.p: TIM JUDGES' REPORT.

Sir William Harcourt, addressing a Liberal meeting at Bath on Wednesday night, said the report of the Parnell Commission was a nine days' wonder. The origin of that Commission was a solecism and a monstrosity, and the English Constitution had never known any- thing like it. He had always designated. " Pamellism and [Crime "as unmitigated rubbish, and this had been now proved to be the case. The bitter poli- tical malignity of the Attorney-General's spee4ti at Oxford showed perfectly well what was the connection of the Government with" Parnellism and Crime." The Commission judges were content to deal with questions If fact, but so far as they had to deal with charges depending on political considerations in his opinion they were wholly unfit for the task. It was amusing to ob- serve the consummate impudence of the " Times" newspaper, which was convicted of the foulest crimes, but they had yet a penalty to pay at the bar of public opinion. The Commission report could do no service to the Unionist party. Sir C. Russell,addressing the Cambridge University Liberal Club on Wednesday night, reviewed the events which the Parnell Commission tad been inquiring into, and the results of that inquiry. Every charge upon which the claim for the Commission had been based, had, 'le said, been found to be disproved. If there had been a conspiracy it had been the conspiracy of a whole people. Their combination was justified by the cruelty of the landlords and the apathy of the Legislature. It dad accomplished its purposes with far less crime than had attached to any previous politimi agitation, and what crime had attended it was due, not to the orga- Msers of the agitation, but to irresponsible and reckless persons found on the fringe of all popular move- ments.

Bribery MR. J. SLATER LEWIS, County and Councillor for the Prodsham Divi- Despotism. sion of Cheshire, has followed up his charges against the County Police by laying the facts before the Home Secretary. Consider- able correspondence has ensued, the principal por- tion of which will be found in another column, but Mr. Lewis cannot be said to have got any satisfac- tion, beyond that which arises from. knowing that he renders a service by exposing the black spots our police system. The Home Secretary shows himself altogether reluctant to go into the case; and well he may, for it relates to practices which show that the dual control of the police is about as bad as any system can possibly be. The corres- . Pondence ought to be carefully preserved by Liberals, whose duty it is never to rest satisfied ; Until those who find the money have the entire control of the men. There is obvious need, too, of hunting the authority of the Chief Constable, or at anY rate taking steps to ensure that his officers Shall not be degraded or dismissed without having ,ft title to a full inquiry into their conduct. Somn of the Tories, instead of be- Tory Tyranny. ing glad, are irritated and dis- appointed at finding from the Re- port of the Parnell Commission that the Parnel- lites have not been guilty of the foul charges brought against them; and they are showing their bad blood and bad breeding in various ways. Lord EGERTON of Tatton has his way. He was applied to as a trustee, the other day, for the use of the High Legh schoolroom for a Liberal meet- ing. In his answer to Mr. J. A. SWANWICK, Chairman of the Lvmm Liberal Association, he admits that it has been customary to let the school to both political parties; but he says:— " I base my refusal on the ground that it is not ' incumbent on the managers of our national schools to give facilities for the support and propagation of such doctrines as those which are now held by the Liberal party,or their avowed allies, Messrs. Parnell ' and other Irish M.P.'s, who, after a judicial investi- gation, impartially carried out, have been declared to be guilty of a 'criminal conspiracy,' as fully set forth in the Report of the Special Commission."
Mr. SWANWICK. in reply, shows himself equal to the occasion. He says—

"As regards your ground for refusal, I cannot but remark that on the only questions fit for "judicial investigation' the Commission has reported abso- lutely in favour of Mr. Parnell and his friends. On the other hand, outside the definite charges, which have all been disproved, nothing is alleged by the Judos which was not perfectly well-known to all the world at the time of the 1885 active alliance between the Conservative party and the Nationalist

The reference to the alliance of 1885 is a home thrust which the Tories cannot and do not deserve to escape. We do not say the alliance was dis- honourable; but it is dishonourtble to turn round on these men and speak' of them, after the fashion of Lord SALISBURY, as though they were Hottentots, or Thugs, when nothing has been proved which was not known when the Tories took them to their arms. Lord EGERTON would doubtless like to be regarded .as a gentleman; but is it the conduct of a gentleman to vent his spite in refusing to let a school when he ought rather to be sympathising with Mr. i'AaNELL for having for Years been un- justly subjected to the foulest charges that could be brought against him either as a politician or as a man? Good, brave "CHRISTOPHER NORTH" once characteristically said—" The animosities are mortal but the humanities are eternal." But Lord EGERTON of Tatton would seem dial osed to dis- tinguish himself by reversing the apothegm. Be it so; it will not be the Nationalists who will thereby be discredited. Dr. Goimaz remarked at Warrington the other week that Toryism was tyranny; be did not think it necessary to quote a modern instance; be left it to Lord EGERTON of Tatton to furnish one. And what of the miser- able feeling which prevents Tory lords and com- moners from owning that they have done wrong in vilifying Mr. PARNELL ? It is, we confess diffi- cult to explain, except on the assumption made by Lord BEACONSFIELD when he said a Tory Govern- ment was an organised hypocriscy. Lord BEACONS- FIELD know, no doubt, what he was talking about.

sale of drink, he is prepared to abolish the system. But I think we can prove that the other branches of the trade are also injurious and ruinous to the public interest ; and I am not without hope that Mr. Gladstone, when he sees that this is proved, will be willing to give the people facilities for their abolition also." And so say all of us.

1 Mr. Chaplin has been caught tripping, and has had to apologise. He started a very pretty story about a compact having been entered into, on the education question, between Mr. John Morley, on behalf of the Liberals, and Mr. T. P. O'Connor, on behalf of the Catholics. He made it out that there had been "close communication" between those gentlemen in the House of Commons, last night week, after Mr. Chamberlain's speech, and that fol- lowing on it Mr. Morley made a statement as to free education in Catholic schools. It transpires that the mare's nest had its origin in Mr. O'Connor sup- plying Mr. Morley with an extract on Free Educa- tion from one of Mr. Chamberlain's speeches

Mr. Chamberlain, by-the-by, has turned a somer- sault upon the education as upon other questions. i Speaking at Inverness, on September 18th, 1885, he said :—"I cannot rest until I see this cruel and abominable tax (i.e., the fee system) abolished, and until every national school is free throughout , the length and breadth of the land." At Bradford, October Ist, 1885, ho said:—" Whenever the time comes for its discussion I, for one, shall not hesitate to express my opinion. The contributions of Government money, whether great or small, ought in all cases to be accompanied by some form of representative control."

The time for discussion came on Friday week, and this is how the member for West Birmingham turned round upon himself : " What they (the free educationists) wanted was popular control; that the Voluntary School Com- mittee should accept a majority of popular repre- sentatives; that to these representatives should be given the full control of the schools; and that the voluntary subscribers to these schools should give up all power into the hands of their new masters. This proposal was, on the face of it, ridiculous.. lie did not say it was undesirable, but he said it Would be ridiculous to suppo,e that the supporters of voluntary schools would accept any such plans. The proposal, in short, like the first which he had examined, was a proposal for the extinction of the voluntary system." Oh Joseph, Joseph, it is most absurd To see you eat your speeches, word by word.
