SUDDEN DEATH AT WIDNES.

John Wright,'4;ciiiie-a:r-si3Of,..VirrTgiii-st., died sud- denly on Sunday morning while following his employ- ment at the works of Mr. E. K. Muspratt. On the previous day, he complained of pains in his chest, but did not appear to be seriously unwell.

"A Living Legacy," an admirable story by Mr. George Manville Fenn, is commenced this week on the second page of the" Examiner."
This is the season of falls through stepping upon orange peel thrown on the footpaths. Policemen would do well to be on the look out; there are altogether too many Orange-men about.

The Irish Loyal and Patriotic Union is certainly not made happy by the Report of the Parnell Commission; for the Secretary Mr, Houston is ousted. He has tendered his resignation and it has been accepted. The new Secretary is Mr. W. Cox. As one cock of the walk did not give satis- faction, the is about to try Cox.

Bellevue prison, Manchester,is about to be offered for sale. Happy thought! Let the electors of East Manchester buy it, and present it to their represontative—the " brave Mr. Balfour." It would be a wonderfully fitting memorial of his Irish administration.

"Brave Balfour" was in a very tight place, on Monday evening, when Mr. Sexton moved the adjournment of the House for the purpose of exposing the shameful way in which 29 workmen were arrested without warrant, because they were engagel at Clongorey in erecting a place of shelter for evicted tenants. The Irish Secretary made a Lime dsi'once; a vote was taken, and the Govern- ment majority wcmt down to 42. A little more of this, and the Government will have no majority at all.

Another case of two lovers being drowned in the Mersey Canal near Dobby's Locks. Oh, the pity of it! A canal bank is not the place for a walk at night, fog or no fog. But the fog on Sunday night was impenetrable--boyonfog the borough lights. It may be that the fog came on whilst the young couple were making their way home by the bank; but there are few ways out, and it will thus be seen how the place may become a death trap.

Unhappily, this was not the only fatal accident through the foggy weather. James Robinson, an old man 77 years of age, was found drowned, on Sunday morning, in Whitley Brook. He left War- rington to walk home on Saturday night, and it is supposed that, bewildered by the fog, he stumbled into the brook and was drowned. Disasters of this kind speak with an emphatic warning voice, and it is to be hoped that in some cases it will not be without effect.

Prepare yourself, reader, for startling intelligence. •—" it is stated by a news agency that the effect of the recommendations of Lord Hartington's Commission on the Army and Navy would be to abolish the office of Commander-in-Chief of the Army. The abolition of the dual control at the Horse Guards finds many supporters, even behind Ministers." What! " Abolish ' the Duke of Cam- bridge! The nation would never survive it! The world would stand still with a rending jar, Like a ship struck at sea.

The annual meetings of the Lancashire Congre- gational Union are to be held, at Blackburn, on Wednesday and Thursday next. The Rev. John Yonge, pastor of Wycliffe Congregational Church, Warrington, is chairman for the present year, and will deliver his presidential address at the opening meeting, on Wednesday. Mr. Yonge is an able and eloquent advocate of Congregational principles, and, as Blackburn is a strong centre of Noncon- formity, it may be taken for granted that he will meet with a most hearty reception. It is not every chairman who is successful in presiding over business meetings, but Mr. Yonge is an exception to the rule; he makes an admirable chairman.

The Secretary for -War was waited upon, on Monday, by a deputation of Lancashire Colonels of, volunteers. Their object was to secure a loan of :C12,000 towards the purchase of the Glazebrook Shooting 'flange ; but all they got was a promise to place the matter before the members of the Cabinet. Something may come of it—another delay perhaps. There is something exceedingly disappointing about the way in which volunteers have towo about, cap in hand, to get what is abso- lutely nYfes3ary for their efficiency as.a force. Why don't they formulate their demands, and show, if they are not complied with, that they, too, like other people, can 0 strike."

A sacred recital was given in the Trinity Wesleyan Chapel on Monday evening, by the choir of St. Paul's, Runcorn, assisted by some of the members of the Run- corn Musie,d Society. Mr. E. div.head: • THE MUZZLING ORDER AT WIDNES!
div.p: • THE MUZZLING ORDER AT WIDNES!

Several persons were summoned to ' Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, for permitting their dogs to be at large unmuzzled. The Chairman of the Bench (Mr. J. Brock) said he had considerable sympathy with persons summoned for this offence, but the magistrates had to carry out the law as laid down. It was, however, very unequal as it at present stood, and the Bench would be as lenient as possible. A fine of Is. and costs 4s. ed. was imposed in each case. Andrew Carragher, of the Arch Hotel, was summoned under the order, but as the dog was a greyhound undergoing exercise, the case was dismissed.

div.head: WIDNES CONSERVATIVE CLUB.
div.p: WIDNES CONSERVATIVE CLUB.

On Thursday evening, a well attended sinoki rig concert was held in the Assembly-room of the Widnes Conseilim- tive Club. Mr. R. Lewis presided, and announced that the Committee had purchased a piano for the entertain- ment of the members on that and future occasions, and the instrument was opened by Misses Lewis and Kyle performing a sole, which was very much applauded. During the evening sons were rendered by Aliases Leach, McCririe. Lea, W. A. Webster, W. E. Smith, Holbrook, W. Kershsw, Welding, Sidney Watkins, T. Atherton, and others. Recitations by Messrs. R. Lewis and W. E Oakden were alto given and much appreciated. The songs were ably accompanied upon the piano by Messrs. E. W. Harrison and W. White. • '

MAD WITH DRINK AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, a rough looking matt named James Smith, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly, and assaulting P.C. Malkin. The constable stated that at half-past eleven on Saturday night, he found the prisoner very drunk and "cursing and swearing at the top of his voice." A crowd had collected amund him. ' Witness requested the prisoner to go home, but he refuseiland struck the officer a blow on the face with his list. A ithiggie ensued and with diffi- culty the prisoner was hand-cuffel and taken to the police station by three officers. Witness stated that the prisoner was more like a madman than anythin., else.— The prisoner alleged that he was quietly looking through a shop window, when the constable came up and knocked him down.—Surrintendent Large,said com- plaints had bvn received of the prisona• anno%ing people.—The prisoner was ordered to pay a fine of 10s. and costs, in each case, or go to gaol for a month.

DRUNKENNESS AND ITS PHYSIOLOGICAL EFFECTS. Under the auspices of St. Patrick's Church, Widnes, on Thursday evening, • the Rev. Father O'Callaghan, of Manchester, delivered a lecture in the Drill Hall, on " Drunkenness and its physiological effect on the. human system." There was A capital attendance and the Rev. Father Nugent occupied the chair. rho Chairman said he was getting an old man and • bad SCOG much of the world, every phase of it high and low, rich and poor,, the labouring man in every condition of labour, and the Intellectual man, and he had vet to meet the ,an, he cared not in what station of life or what office he filled, he had yet to meet the man that would not be a better man without intoxicaiing drink than with it. (Applause ) The Rev. Fattier o*(elaghan theta delivered-his lecture,.! and at the conclusion he was cordially thanked On the motion of Mr. E. Carey, seconded by Dr. O'Donnell. A similar compliment was paid to Father Nugent. IRISH NATIONAL LRAGUE, WIDNES. A meeting of the members of the Widnes branch of the Irish National League, was held in the Leave room, on Sunday afternoon. Mr. Nolan, presided. Mr. Del Iney proposed " That we the Irishmen of Widnes, in union , with the rest of our fellow countrymen throughout the world, wish to express our heartfelt sorrow at the death of Joseph C. fligga.r, the brave ano patriotic member Lir Cavan, who for the last 16 years has donegood and noble service, both inside and outside Parliament. We tender to his friends and relative our deep sympathy with them in their bereavement by the loss of one whom they in 1 Ireland loved so well. It had pleased Providence to call. Mr. Biggar from the trials and difficulties of this world, to* the land where there is no obstruction and where peace, ease, and happiness awaits all who, as Mr. Biggar had done, had forwarded the cause of GAI and his country." The resolution was seConded by the Chair- man supported by Mr. J. G. Taggar and C.C. of Liver- pool, and wa.: carried unanitnon4y. 'PRE ACTOR AND HIS DOG AT RUNCORN. . " •

• Vere Montague, an actor at the Theitre Royal, ap- peared before the Runcorn magistrates, on M'lnday morning*, to answer R ehargciof allowing his dog to roam at large inite%nr,ly muzzled. On the 17th inst. P.C. Worinrow saw lie defecdant with , a couple of " ladies " hiChurch-st. They were accompanied bye deg, which. although it had a muzzle on, was carrying the head of a fish in its mouth. He pointed thisout to the defendant, whereupon one of the "ladies" asked "What the—it had gat to do with him." He informed them he was a policeman, but the defendant refused to give his name. —Superintendent Large stated that the defendant brought the dog to the Police Station, and the muzzle was so loose he could easily have placed his hand in its mouth. Defendant said he had been in several towns and there had been no complaints about the dog's muzzle until he came to Runcorn. A fine of 6d. and costs 10s. 64. was imposed. The defendant now wished the case adjourned f9r a week, and on being told that it was dealt with, he asked if he could appeal.—P.S. Gosling told him to pay his fine first and then appeal, and the defendant growling about the injustice of the whole proceedings, handed over the required sum.

WIDNES CHEMICAL LABOURERS' UNION. Mr. T. J. King is actively continuing his work of organising this union, and encouraging success is attend- ing efforts. He has addressed large meetings each evening during the week, with the exception of Tuesday, and considerable numbers of workmen have enrolled themselves as members. Mr. King has stated that he understood one of the contractors, who are generally known as lumpers, had granted a rise of 6d. per day to his men,•and this showed what the Union was likely to do for the men. In his addresses Mr. King announces that he is prepared to take the part of the men against all corners and, as a reasonable feeling existed amongst the men, it would be for the masters to exhibit a like feeling. The masters would indeed be foolish if they refused to take advantage of the present conciliatory spirit, which prevailed among the men, for by reason- able treatment, these men who were obliged to labour for them would take a greater interest in their work and prove to the -masters that they would lose nothing by any concession they might grant them.—Mr. King has also addressed a meeting of tte Flatmen and Narrow Boat- men's Union, and of the Salt 'Worker's Union at Runcorn, pointing out the benefits of Union, and promising that he would endeavour to bring about a federation of all the trades' Unions of the district ; but he advised them to at present proceed on their own lines, by which they had achieved considerable saccess. 100 members have been enrolled during the past week. A DIVING "SELL" AT RUNCORN. For some days previous to Sunday, a man named Thomas Dawson, or Dovsey, had been loudly proclaim- ing his intention of diving from Runcorn Bridge, into the Mersey at three o'clock on Sunday, afterwards walking to London and back in six days. According to Dawson's own statement he was a " champion " swimmer and runner, but he had apparently ',sunk in the scale of human progress, for during the few weeks he had been in Runcorn, he had earned a. precarious living as a gatherer of rags, and had lived in a common lodging- house. In anticipation of seeing his aerial flight of about 80 feet. people in hupdreds from the surrounding towns, and at the time fixed fully six thousand per- sons were gathered on the Lancashire and Cheshire banks of the river. Dawson, however, had evidently repented of his rash vow and did not put in an appear- ance, much to the disgust of the assembled multitude who after partially waiting an hour and a half, quietly dispersed 4 Tommy Burns, who is now known as "the Runcorn Bridge hero" was present on the lofty struc- ture to see Dawson's performance and prepared to eclipse by a still more daring exhibition of his diving abilities than he has hitherto displayed from the Bridge. As it was he was much tempted tc give the spectators a taste of his prowess so that they should not be altogether disappointed, but he said he had never worked on a Sun- day yet, and as there was no necessity owing to Daw- son's retreat, he resisted the temptation. Dawson has since written a letter from Northwich to the lodging house keeper saying he would send some " monie evi- dently to pay off an old score. A 4DICLIGHTFUL FLAVOUR. div.head: VISIT OF Mk. THOMAS CHAMPNEYS TO RUNCORN.
div.p: VISIT OF Mk. THOMAS CHAMPNEYS TO RUNCORN.

It is announced that Mr. Thomas Champneys, founder of tile " Joyful News " Mission, will visit St. Paul's Chapel, Runcorn, on Thursday, the 13th March. H. :will preach in the afternoon, and address a public meet- ing in the evening.

SODDEN DEATH AT WIDNES. Jaines Tyrell, stonebreaker, 64 years of age, of 24, Market-st , was found dead in bed on Wednesday morn- ing. He was seized with a cold on Sunday last, and did not go to his work on Monday or Tuesday in consequence but no serious results were apprehended. The man had not been attended by a doctor for two years. STRIKE OF WORKMEN AT WIDNES. On Thursday morning the joiners employed at the works of Messrs. James Muspratt and Sons Chemical Works, struck work for an advance of wages. At present the men work 54 hours a week for 285., and they ask for ,sxn advance of ss. per week, which the masters have re- fused to grant. The dischargers at the works of Messrs. Hutchinson and Co., have also gone out on strike. They claim to have their wages increased from 3s. 6d. to 4s. per day. The dischargers at Messrs. Golding, Davies and Co's. Works have also struck for an additional 6d. per day. In this instance the men are paid 4s. per day at-present. The labourers at the Tharsis Copper Co's. Works have also turned out, because their demlnd for an increase of wages has not been conceded. Ry these strikes many other men at the works have been thrownnut of employment. Yesterday, a meeting of manufacturers was held at the Central Hotel for the purpose of ascertaining the wages paid by different firms for similar classes of work. There were about 20 representatives present, and we understand that an effort will be made to adopt a uniform scale of wages.

" GREAT EXPECTATIONS" IN CILESHIRE. Lord Thurlow presided at the meeting of the Salt Union on Thursday, and stated that on their pro- perty in Cheshire they were boring for coal and other minerals, and he believed they were on the eve of the discovory of coal, perhaps petroleum, and natural gas in Cheshire greater than the expected discovery of coal in Bent, and which, if realised, would double or treble the value of their property.
BASINETTEI, new Ilesigns,—Garlaud, Ironmonger, War- rington.--Add. FOUND DEAD IN THE STREETS.__

A painful discovery was made at St. Helens, on Thursday morning, when the dead body of a man unknown was found lying in l'easley Cross-lane, about half-past four °clock. It is that of a man about forty years of age, 5 feet Bor 9 inches. He had in his possesion three pawntickets for articles pledged in the name of Benjamin Smith, and one pawnticket in the name of James Richards, pledged with Washington Hargreaves, Wellington-st., Scholes, Wigan. • The body was taken to the public mortuary in Mary-st., where it lies awaiting identi- fication. -

MIRING OPERATIONS NEA.R. ST. HELENS. _ THE PARCEL POST BETWEEN LIVERPOOL AND

_ MANCILESTSIE. We learn that the con; ract for the horsing of the I postal parcel coaches. which are to run between Manchester and Liverpool. has been let to a Man- chester firm—Messrs. Wood Brothers, horse dealers and auctioneers, Dut Strangeways. The vehicles are now being built, and it is expected that a start with the new system will be made about the second week in April. There is no intention of sending mails by the road. They will, as hereto- fore, he despatched by rail. The vans will carry parcels only. It is no secret that the postal autho- rities are not satisfied with the arrangement with the railway companies for th e co nv eyance of parcels. The companies take 55 per cent. of the payments made by the public, leaving the Post Office to' under- take: collection, cartage to and from railway sta- tions, and distribution to remote places for the re- maining 45 per cent. In the judgment of the Post- master and other officials of the department the arrangement ought at least to be reversed, the Post Office taking 55 per cent. and the railway people the lesser portion. REGISTER GRATES.—J. S. Garland, 51, urldge-street, War rington.—Advt. RICHARD 'EVANS AND CO., LIMITED. The first report of the directors of Richard Evans and Co., Limited, which was formea last year for the purpose of taking over and working the exten- sive collieries belonging to the late Mr. Richard Evans, at Hay dock, Golborne, Ashton, &c., has just been issued to the shareholders. The new company took over,the concern from the Ist of June, 1889,and kilt) accounts are made up to the 31st of December last. The report says : "There have been issued 43,502 A shares. 15,979 B shares, and 2,750 £lOO Five Per Cent. Debenture. The share list has been closed." The accounts of the company are neces- sarily meagre, as they can only be completed up to the end of December, and :show the amounts re- ceived and paid respectively to that date. The out- put of the collieries for the seven months ending 31st December last amounted to abom 750,000 tons. The directors are glad to report that there has been considerable improvement in the coal trade gener- ally. and they look forward with great hope to its continuance, and confidently anticipate that the re- sult of the current year's workingwill not be unsatis- factory to the shareholders. The balance" sheet shows a profit on the seven months' working £26,984 Sc. 7d. UMBRELLLS RE-COVERED at an hours' nottce.TJ. & W. Dutton, dankev-street. THE FRBB EDUCATION DIVISION.

TO MIL STANHOPE.

A deputation from Lancashire colonels of vaun- teers waited, on Monday, upon Mr. E. Stanhope, M.P., Secretary for War, and asked that the Gov- ernment should advance a loau toward the purchase of the Glazebrook shooting range. Colonel Blundell, M.P., introduced the deputation, and Mr. Hard- castle, M.P., Colonel Bridfork Colonel Greenall, and Colonel Lynd poiuted out how difficult it had been to find a imitable range, and how necessary it was to secure the one at Glazehrook. The sum required was £12,000, but there would be ample security, for the amount earned by the Government grant was £14,000, and there was also the additional value of the various headquarters. If the scheme fell through it would be a serious deterrent to the volunteers of the district. Colonel Greenall said that about eight years ago a range was taken from his regiment after it had been in use 27 years, and the whole of the money spent upon the range, amounting to £1,500, was lost. The regiment was now using a range at Widnes; but they might be turned out of it any day. lie did not know where to look for a range, and it was hopeless to think that it would turn up unexpectedly afterlthey had been sifting the matter for seven years. if the present proposal failed, volunteers would be deterred from joining the battalion. Mr. Stanhope, in reply, said the matter was one of considerable urgency, and with the new rifle would be more important still. He would place the request of the deputation before his colleagues in strong terms, and every- thing he could do to maintain the efficiency of the brigade strAild be done. The brigade had reached a high state of efficiency, and it would be a pity if the efficiency of the Manchester regiments was not maintained. Sir*. liouldsworth, M.P.; in thanking the Secretary for War, said there was a strong feel- ing in Lancashire that the Government should advance the loan. _ .

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. Colonel Ashton presided, and there were present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. E. Aaron, J. Weir,P. Hall, J. Lewir, J. Smith, J. Brandreth, Bretherton, J. Hall, T. Forster, J. Stokes, Dr. Adams (medical officer), H. Linaker (clerk), and H. G. Linuker (assistant clerk). MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. The Medical Ofricer of Heal.h presented his annual re- port in which he stated that the rural sanitary district , contained 36 townships, with 45,941 acres, and the census population in 1881 was 18,892. Be estimated that the population at the present time was 22,112. During the past year there had been 673 births and 377 deaths, including those which occurred in the Work- house. Of the deaths 31 formed the subject of coroners' inquiries, while eiebt were returned as " uncertified : Ino medical attendant." Both these figures were very high. The birth rate was 30.6 per 1.030 per annum of the estimated population compared with 31 per 1,000 in 1888. The death rate was 17.1 per 1,000 perannum of the estnnated population, compared with the death rate of 144 in 1888. Of the 377 d-aths 90 oc :Lured amongst children under one year; 44 between one and five years; 14 between 5 and 15; 12 between 15 and 25; 89 .between 25 and 60 • 50 between 60 and 70 years of age • 33 of which were males and 19 females; 51 occoired between 70 and 80, 25 of which were males and 26 females; 24 occurred in persons between 80 and 90, nine of which were males and 15 feinaks ; While one man, a watchman at Weston Point, reached the age of 92 summers. Forty-seven deaths occiirred from zymotic diseases, of which 17 were from whooping cough, 6 from typhoid fever; and 16 from diarrhoea and. dysentery. These figures yielded 12.4 percent. of the total, deaths compared with 12 per cent. in 1888. The zymotic death rate was 2.1 per 1,000. Hut for the whooping cough epidemic they would have had an exceedingly • low zymotic deatn rate. Fhthisis caused 27 deaths; bronchitis pneumonia and pleurisy, 89 ; heart disease, 24 ; accidents and violence, 21. ; all other diseases 169.—The report was adopted, and srdered to be printed by tender as usual.

The directors reported that during the past twelve months they had disposed of twelve houses situate on Lower Long Croft Estate for the amount for which they. were in mortgage to the company, also the freehold land on which they stood as under ,—No. 3, £234 11s. One house in York-st., and six houses in Crown-st., had been dis- posed of, with the freehold of the land, for the sum of £1,575. The directors intended to devote the realized assets to develop the company's lands in the erection of property thereon, and had already made an agreement or the erection o ten houses on Lower Long Croft Estate, and purpose building other blocks of property on the Greenway-road estate as soon as satisfactory arrange- ments could be made with contractors. The report was adopted, and the chair- man was re-elected a director. Mr. W. Rock, chartered accountant, Widnes, was re-appointed auditor. RUNCORN W.vrEltwoims COMPANY. The half-yearly rno,lititz of the elutrehoidere of the Runcorn. We,ton, ail Halton Waterworks Company, was held at. the Public 'Hall, on Alonday afternoon. Mr. J. Brundrit, J.P., presided, and there were present Messrs. Time. • Bankes, John Simpson, Wm. Whittaker, Wm. Hayes, Ebenezer Timmins, Si Taylor, P. Smith, W. F. Saikeld (sec.), and VV. Jemes (assistant secretary). The directors repo& stated :—" The Revenue account shows a balance of £855 2s. 9d.. including £77 Bs. Bd., brought from the previous half-year, out of which the directors recommend dividsnd to be declared of 31 per centum per annum, free from income tax, payable on and after the Ist day of March ; this will absorb £487 10s., leaving a balance of ~£lB7 12s. 9d., to be carried forward. The engines at the. • Pumping Station having been in use , mere than twenty years require considerable ro- il pairs, which are proceedinl with despatch and 'economy combined with efficiency. The water in the well continues as previously and of good quality." The Secretary having read the auditor's certificate of the correctness of the accounts, the Chairman proposed the adoption of the report and the declaration of the divi- dend recommended, and remarked that the dividend was not as satisfactory as they hail hoped it would have been ; but they were carrying forward a larger balance in order to meet the charge for the repair of the engines out of re.enue. The engines had been examined by two practical engineers and their reports were practically alike, and it was on their recommendation that extensive repairs were being made. There had been a diminution in the receipts caused by the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company and the London and North-Western Railway Cempany using a less amount of water than usual, but the former works were now in full operation after a temporary stoppage caused by re-fixing some of their plant and the C-ompany were again supplying the works with a great quantity of water. When the engines were repaired. the directors would have nothing to do except ordinary renewal for a considerable number of years, the expenses would be lightened, and thev would be in a more satisfactory position to conduct the business of the Company. The water continued good and there were no complaints of scarcity from any part of the town.—Mr. Bankes seconded the motion which was carried unanimously. On the motion of Mr. Smith seconded by Mr. favlor, a vote of thanks was accorded to the chairman and directors for their services, and the meeting terminated.

ALLEGED CRUELTY TO A BOY AT FRODSITAIL At RidisturY Petty Sessions, on Monday. John Aston, an elderly man, residing at Frodsham, was summoned for an assault on his grandson, Fred Aston.—The Rev. 11. B. Blogg, vicar of Frodsham, stated that as he was passing close to th":lefend- ant's house, on February 14th, he heard a noise and a child crying as though in great pain. He entered the residence and found Aston kicking his grandson in a most vicious manner. He stopped him and told him it VMS a most brutal and cowardly thing to do, and would have a summons issued against him. This sort of thing had been going on for some time, and in the in- terests of the boy he thought it only right to summon the gefendant. The boy was thirteen years of age, but he did not look more than ten. The child's mother was believed to be in America, Be thought there was a good deal of ill-treatment going, on, and it seemed to be his duty to 'protect children as far as possible. He would suggest that the old man was not a proper person to have control of the lad, h(mce be was quite prepared to admit him into the Kingsley Home, and see that he did not suffer in the way he at present did through ill- treatment.—Mrs. Ellen Janion,aneighbour, said she had frequently heard the boy's cries. On one occasion she saw him leap through the bedroom window into the lane, and on another day she saw him jammed between the door and the posts. Defendant thrashed the boy unmercifully it times.—Defendant made a lung state- ment as to how the boy Icrd been under his care since a child, a few months old, when he was deserted :how he had been a bcliringer at the Parish Church for 54 years

how he had provided the boy a comfortable horn.; and how chat on the day in question he was thrashing him for disobeying orders. What he had done was for the boy's ultimate good. He promised that in future his grandson should be treated in a manner not calling for complaint from anyone.—The Chairman said they could not carry out the suggestion of the rev, gentleman as to sending the boy to Kingsley Home, under the present summons, which was for assault, and not for the preven- tion of cruelty to children.—Mr. Higson said he was sure the parish must be greatly indebted to Mr. Blogg for the trouble he had taken in that case, in order that justice might be done.—The defendant was ordered to pay 4s. 6d. costs, and warned that if he was brought up again tor similar conduct, the boy would be takon from under his charge. div.head: FINANCES. A NINEPENNY RATE,
div.p: THE FINANCES. A NINEPENNY RATE,

Mr. Brandreth presented the report of the Finance Committee, who recommended that the County Council be paid £2,036 on account of £4,706 demanded. That sum was what the Boardestimated would be required by the County Council. It was a question whether the Council would receive it, but of course they would try them.—The Rev. J. W. N Tanner: And trust them.— The recommendation was adopted.—The estimate of the probable expenditure for the half-year eudingiMichaelmas next, was also submitted. The total capital for the current half-year ending Lady Day. 1890, amounted to £6,931, and the nett probable expenditure was estimated at £7,902, which showed a deficit of £971. The pro- bable expenditure for the next half-year, including the deficit and a sum to give back the usual balance of one penny in the £, was £8,384, the particulars being, school fees for non-pauper children, £43; common charges, £3,405; county rate, £2,271; balance and con- tingency fund,£l,694. The rateable value ot the Union was £217,919, being an increase of £682 ,as compared with Michaelmas, 1889, and an increase of £949 as com- pared with the ,corresponding period last year. The Manchester Ship Canal Company had had a large rate- able value struck out the valuation lists Upon which they make up the deficiency in th e poor rates,and this accounted for the apparently small increase in the rateable value as compared with previous years. A rate of 9d. in the £ produced the sum of £8,262 and it was recommended that a call of 9d. in the £, he made upon the overseers being an increase of id. in the £, compared with the corresponding period of last year. Since this report was written, an increased rateable value on the several lines of railway in the union had been arranged with the Com- panics 0t£2,399 ; thus making the rateable value of the Union £220,318, or an increase of £3,348 as compared with the corresponding period of last year. Mr. Aaron asked whether the Board could compel the County Coun- cil to pay the sum they owed the Union? Mr. Weir We cam put them in the County Court for it—The Assistant Clerk said the amount to be received from the Council in aid of salaries under the Local Government Act, 1888, was £1,832. They were obliged to pay the Union that amount.—Mr. Aaron asked whether they were likely to have another call from the Council for £4,000 to be paid in five weeks.—Mr. Brandreth said the Clerk to the Council in reply to a request had intimated that the Council would not probably require more than 2d. in the £, for the next half year.—Mt Aaron said perhaps the Clerk wrote without the authority of the Council, same as lie did at the last meeting.—The Clerk said the clerk had answered to the best of his knowledge and he made up the accounts.—Mr. Brandrith said they must trust the officials, and proposed the adoption of the estimate. The motion was seconded and carried.
There was no other business of public interest.

THE WONDER OF WESTERN AUSTRALIA.

In the year 1856, Joseph Pyke, with his wife and two young children, sailed from London for Australia. He was a journeyman shoemaker, and so poor, that if his passage had not been a gift, he could not have gone at all. The passage was long in those days of sailing ships, and his vessel—after having been nearly wrecked off the • Cape—consumed five months in reaching that far-off and then almost unknown country. In England he often had to earn the pennies for his breakfast before he was allowed to have it; but in the new land his condi- tion gradually changed for the better. Finding that farming combined with shopkeeping was likely to pay better than shoemaking:he took up land under the easy terms provided by law, and began making a home for himself. He raised corn and sheep, and sold goods to the rude people of his section. Being industrious, ener- getit, and sober, he prospered. We should not omit to mention that on the passage he earned a few pounds by - cobbling shoes, and this money was all the capital he had to start with. What was still more discouraging, poor Pyke was handicapped by chmnic illness. Through his hard life since boyhood he had contracted indigestion and dyspepsia, for which he had never been able to obtain a cure. Indeed, he vas now scarcely more than a boy, only twenty-four years old, and a stranger in a country at that time virtually a wilderness and exile for convicts.

But Pyke was plucky. He had a strain of the genuine old Engish grit, which has helped so many of his country- • men to conquer obstacles. When he left home he seemed to have a tendency to consumption, and the doctor said, "Pyke, you may go to Australia, but it wont't save you. I give you about five months to live. You'll probably arrive just about in time to find a grave in the ground instead of in the water." Bat the doctor wag wrong, as doctors often are. The change from the damp, cold climate of England to the half-tropical climate of the great South- ern Continent was somewhat beneficial; but the radical ailment from which he suffered remained. With every change of weather he would have an attack. In a land of plenty he nearly starved, because he could not eat without feeling all the pangs of acute dyspepsia. Physi- -clans were rare birds in Australia in 1956, but Pyke didn't lament on that account, as they had done him no 'especial good in a country where they were more abun- dant than shoemakers. So he did his best to forget he was not a well man, and went on making his fortune. lie built a good house, and added land to land until his great farm stretched away on every side like a whole county in England ; for Australia is so large that a piece of ground the sizeof this whole island would hardly be missed out of it, and so fertile that wealth is certain to reward everybody who will work. But while land and sheep, and money accumulated as time went by, our friend Pyke kept losing wl:at is more valuable than either—health and strength. Although he was lord of the manor, he was physically a very little lord, as he weighed only seven stone. Yet a better time was coming, and the means by which he was to reach it was then on its way from England. One day a small packet of pamphlets arrived at the post-office when he received his mail, and one of them fell into his hands. As soon as he saw what it was about he read it eagerly. Among its contents was a simply-written account of the malady called indigestion and dyspepsia. All the symptoms he had been tormented with since his young manhood were so clearly described that he recognised every one of them, like the faces of familar enemies. 'There were also verified statements of cases astad or worse than his own, having been cured by a preparation named Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. But this awoke hope only to throw a shadow over it ; for how on earth Was he to get this medicine ? England was too far away, and so far as he then knew there was not a drop of it in Australia. Presently, however, he found out that there was Whence that a shopkeeper seventy miles away might have it. Seventy miles was nothing when life and health were the goal to the race to be run. He travelled that distance, and to his unbounded delight he obtained several bottles, carried them home more carefully than if they were nuggets of gold, took the contents as directed by the book, and in a short time gained a degree of health, strength, and vigour he had never known be- fore.

In August, 1889, Mr. Pyke, ex-Mayor of York, where be now owns large business interests, and one of the most successful and influential men in Western Australia, visited London, when he laid the above facts before the writer cf this article. Said he," lam proud of Austra- lia and of what it has done for me, and prouder still of Seizel's Syrup, which, mdre than anything in the climate, has made me what I am. When they allude to Little Pyke,' astbey used to call me, they now add the words, The Wonder of Western Australia! If that 'medicine couldn't be had for less money, I would freely -give £lOO a bottle for it."

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRITEB.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRITEB.

AN UNGRATEFUL BOY. A lad named John Grimn was before the Warrington mazistrates on Monday, when a tale of ingratitude was related. Mrs. Ward, who keeps a refreshment house in Peter-st., had supplied him with food nearly all the winter, and he repaid the kindness by stealing some coppers from the shop till. The magistrates sent Grinni to jail for a month, but as he was in a weak state of health he was not ordered to undergo hard labour.

div.head: . ROBBERY BY A GIRL.-A SAD CASE.
div.p: . ROBBERY BY A GIRL.-A SAD CASE.

Yesterday morning, at the Warrington Police Court., a little girl named Mary Urmston, who is in her fourteenth year, the daughter of a forge labourer living in Turner- street, was brought up on a charge of having stolen a purse containing 18s. 2d. in cash, and two Co-operative checks, valued 10d., from the dress-pocket of Margaret Ann Hughes, on the previous night. She pleaded guilty She took the purse from Mrs. Hughes' pocket, and when in custody admitted having ccmmitted other thefts. The magistrates sent the girl to prison for a fortnight, to be followed by three years' detention ma reformat9ry. •
A TRIVIAL CHARGE OF ASSAULT.

Yesterday morning, at the Warrington Police Court, a boy named Fred Smith was summoned for having assaulted another boy named James Henry Thornton, son of Mr. Henry Thornton, on 17th February. Com- plainant said that as he was going home on the date in question defendant threw something that hit him in the eye. It did not make the eye black, make it bleed, or hurt him. liefendant said that he and other boys were playing, and a piece of soft bark that he threw hit the complainant, but the occur- rence was accidental. It also transpired that the defend- ant had been to Mr. Thornton and tendered an apology. Alderman Harrison, in dismissing the case, said that to have summoned the defendant seemed to be a very frivolous course to take. What offence there was was wholly inadequate to the annoyance that the defendant and his mother must have suffered from the proceedings Theproper course would have been to accept the apology

div.head: MUZZLING ORDER.
div.p: THE MUZZLING ORDER.

At he Warrington Polico Court, on Monday morning, Henry Bowers, of Cairo-st., was summoned for having allowed his dog to be at large and unmuzzled on the 15th February. It was alleged that whilst in the Public Hall Hotel, the defendant removed the muzzle from his dog, and the animal, taking advantage of its temporary release, bit a girl on the leg. The wound was afterwards cauterized by a surgeon. A fine of is. and costs was inflicted, and the defendant, on the suggestion of the presiding magistrate, Alderman Davies, agreed to pay ss. towards the doctor's fee. He observed that that was the second medical fee he had paid, ashe took the girl to his own doctor, after she had been taken by her mother to another medical man. He averred that the dog only scratched the girl, and did not bite her. A MANCHESTER MARINE STORE DEALER ROBBER.

Patrick O'Hare, a marine store dealer, of 26, Ludgate- hill, Manchester, attended at the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, to prefer a charge of robbery against a navvy named Thomas Donnelly, who was brought up in custody. Be alleged that Donnelly had stolen from him the sum of £1 195., in the early hours of Monday morning. O'Hare came to Warrington on Saturday, and putlip at Mullholland's lodging-house, Mersey-street, whde the prisoner had been living for some time. Pro- secutor spent Sunday in drinking, and just before clos- ing time he gave prisoner 2s. 6d. to fetch some beer. The drink was brought, and distributed between the_occu- pants of the house. In the middle of the night prosecu- tor complained that he had been robbed. Mrs. Mull- holland called in Constables Davies and Hughes, who found that most of the occupants were drunk, the pri- soner being the most sober person in the house. He at at first said he had no money on him, but afterwards admitted that he had 14s. ; on his being searched £2 133. 1.4 d. was found in his possession. Several other persons were searched, amongst them being prosecutor,on whom only £1 18s. was found, whereas 24 hours before he had over £l5. In defence prisoner said that the prosecutor had given him £2 to take care of for him. The Bench were satisfied that the charge had been proved, and com- mitted Donnelly to prison for a month,with hard labour.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 1, 1890.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 1, 1890.

doubt, therefore, they were on very friendly terms. Therehas not been a word or a whisper to the contrary. Theytwere walking in the neighbourhood, and were pro- bably crossing the bridge, and if it was left open in the way which has been described, the night being dark and foggy, the presumption is that they would walk together into the canal. The man Collins heard a shout, and he ran towards the place; but, unfortunately, in the dark he stumbled over a sheep, and that would delay him somewhat. He got a light, but all was then over. The question is "How did they get into the water—by acci- dent, or by throwing themselves in 2" The last-named is particularly improbable. In this case you can, if you prefer it, return an open verdict. The inference is that the parties walked into the water and that they came by their death by accident. If, however, you are not satis- fied, you would be justified in returning an open verdict of "Found dead." Had the footpath been a public one it would have been your duty to inquire by whose negli- gence the bridge was left open. It was a private way, and consequently these people had no right there.—The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased were accidentally drowned, and a juror, Mr. J. Hough- ton, observed that they were not the first couple who had been lost at that place. It was a place where people go sweethearting,,, but it was foolish to go there on a dark and foggy night. BRAVE RESCUE BY A POLICEMAN. Shortly after nine o'clock on Monday evening, a lady and gentleman who were passing over Black Bear Bridge, Latchford, observed a man who seemed the worse for drink leaveithe road and go along the towing path of the Old Quay Canal. Fearing that he might come to some harm they drew the attention of P.C. Rowbotham, whom they met close by, to the matter. The Constable hurried to the canal side, and just as he reached it he heard a cry for help and saw the man disappear beneath the water. Hastily divesting himself of coat and helmet he jumped into the water, and, with the assistance of the landlords of the Brook and Black Bear Inns, suc- ceeded in bringing the man to the bank. When rescued the man was in an apparently lifeless condition, but after proper attention, recovered sufficiently to be re- moved to his home. He gave his name and residence as William Dakin, Top Locks, Latchford. Constable Row- botham has already achieved distinction as a saver of life, for he holds a Royal Society's medal tor similar heroic conduct whilst serving as a soldier in Egypt. He also holds several military medals. AN UNPLEASANT EXPERIENCE. During the fog on Sunday night, a man named &an Bond, an army pensioner, whose home is at Statham, was walking near Statham Bridge, when he accidentally fell into the'Bridgewater Canal. Very fortunately he was able to extricate himself from his perilous predicament, and he proceeded home not seriously the worse for the mishap. DROWNED IN A BROOK AT WHITLEY. _

Mr. Robert Dobson deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Nook House, Antrobus, on Monday, touching the death of a farm labourer named James Robinson, whose bOdv was found in Whitley Brook on Sunday morning. Evidence was adduced to the effect that the deceased, who was 77 years of age, was on his way home on Saturday evening. The weather at the time was foggy, and, from the footprints which were afterwards observed on the path by the aide of the brook, it is surmised that Robinson lost his way and fell into the water. His body was discovered on the following morning. The jury re- turned a verdict of "Death from misadventure. • A_ WARRINGTON SOLDIER DROWNED. . _

A soldier of the South Lancashire Regiment, stationed in Jersey, is reported to have been acci- dentally drowned on Saturday afternoon. He was out fishing, and was surrounded by the rising tide on the rocks in St. Owen's Bay, and he has not been seen since. The missing man, who was named Orimshaw, enlisted at Warrington, and had been in the island only a few days.

div.head: SERIES OF ACCIDENTS.
div.p: A SERIES OF ACCIDENTS.
FOUR PERSONS DROWNED.
PLUCKY CONDUCT OF A POLICEMAN.

The past few days have, been very prolific of sorrow to the members of several families in the neighbourhood of Warrington. During the thick fog that prevailed oo Sunday night, a couple of lovers, who were enjoying each others companion- ship, accidentally walked into the canal at a spot near Dobby's locks, and were drowned ; an old man named Robinson was drowned, on Saturday night, in a brook at Whitley, where his body was found next morning; and on Saturday also a Warrington soldier, who was stationed with his,regiment—the South Lancashire—at Jersey, was drowned whilst out on a fishing expedition. These fatalities have naturally occasioned some excitement in the neigh- bourhood, and the relatives of the young man and woman who met so tragic a fate, on Sundai, have been the recipients of very widespread sympathy. A man named Bond, while walking near the canal at Statham. on Sunday night, accidentally fell or waked into the water during the fog, but he man- aged to get out again without assistance. On Morolay night, a young man had a very narrow escape from drowning in the canal near Black Bear Bridge, at Latchford. and his name would almost of a certainty have figured in the sad li of deaths this week, had it not been for the plucky conduct of a policeman, who jumped into the water and effected a rescue at considerable risk to himself. Particulars in detail of the events mentioned are appsnded. LOVERS DROWNED DURING THE FOG.

The couple who were drowned near Debby's Locks on Sunday night were engaged lovers, and were each about the same age—twenty years. Their names were Robert Barnett and Edith Lowe. Barnett, who was a steady young fellow, lived with an aunt at 77 Buttermarket-st., and was by occupa- tion a tripe-dresser, he being employed in that capa- city by Mr. T. Mayhall, of Butterrnarket. His sweet- heart was a four-loom weaver at Cockhedge-mill, and lived with her parents at 15 Greenall-at., her father being a butcher. The couple, both very re- spectable young persons, had been courting for some months and like most lovers, they had their favour- ite walk. Unfortunately for them, as it has.proved, their particular choice had fallen upon the water side at Howley, in the direction of Woolston, where they were accustomed to take occasional strolls. On Sunday night there was a thick fog prevailing over the neighbourhood, but it would seem that the lovers, were not deterred by the fact from venturing on a walk that could not be otherwise than danger- ous under such conditions. No suggestion has been made, and there have beers no grounds upon which any could be made, that the tragic death of Barnett and Lowe was anything but an accident, but it is beyond question that they acted very im- prudently in taking such a walk on such a night. They have paid the penalty .of this rashness with their lives, and it is to be hoped that their fate will prove a lasting warning to any others who may be inclined to be equally im- prudent. The deceased were evidently on good terms on the night of the accident, and they were met and spoken to by the sister of the young man, when in Bridge-street, before proceeding on their walk. Barnett's absence from home was not observed until the following mining, when one of the family went to his room to awaken him. It was then seen that his bed had not been slept in, and the alorm which till§ discovery- occasioned was soon afterwards increased by the arrival of a mes- senger from the parents of tha young woman, seek- ing news of their daughter, who, also, had not been at home all night. It subsequently transpired that on Sunday night a young man named John Collins, who was one of the principal witnesses at the in- quest, was in the vicinity of the canal when he hoard a cry for help apparently in a female's voice. I He set off running towards the spot whence the cry seemed to come, but, in consequence of the fog, he fell over a sheep that he had not been able to see, and this slightly delayed his progress. When he reached the canal he could 800 no signs of anyone struggling in the water, but found an umbrella on the path. He then did the best possible thing under the circumstances, and informed Sergeant Barnes, at Padgate Police Station, of the matter. Early next morning the sergeant proceeded to t,he spot, where a hat, afterwards identified as belong- ing to the young man, was found floating on the water. Dragging operations were commenced, it being thought beyond the possibility of doubt that the unfortunate couple had been drowned, and shortly before eleven o'clock both bodies were re- covered, one being found about ten minutes after the other. The watch in Barnett's pocket had stopped at nine o'clock. Intelligence of the dis- covery was at once conveyed to the friends of the deceased, and the bodies were removed to the Dog and Partridge Inn, there to await an inquest.

, THE INQUEST. Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputylcoroner for South- West Lancashire, held an inquiry into the circumstances of the sad occurrence at the Dog and Partridge Inn, Poulton, on the afternoon of Wednesday. Mr. James Evans watched the proceedings on behalf of the Man- chester Ship Canal Company, Bridgewater Canals under- taking.

div.head: EVMHFCH OF IDHNTITY .
div.p: EVMHFCH OF IDHNTITY .

The first witness called was James Lowe, butcher, 15, Greenail-st., who had identified the body of the female deceased as that of his daughter, Edith Lowe, who was 20 years of age. She was, he said, a weaver, and had resided with witness and her mother. He last saw her alive between five and six o'clock on Sunday evening. She was engaged to be married to Robert Barnett. Wit- ness, who seemed much distressed,added that he was not present when his daughter's body was found. He identi- fied the umbrella produced as having belonged to her. —Frances Barnett, domestic servant,Crown Inn, Butter- market-st., then gave evidence of identification respect- ing the other body, which she recognized as that of her brother. He was a tripe dresser, and lived with his parents at 77, Buttermarket-at. About half-past seven o'clock on Sunday evening, she saw him at Market-gate with Edith Lowe. She spoke to them, and they said they were going for a walk as far as the bridge. By that she understood Warrington Btidge. Her brother was 21 years of age. She said "good night," and left them. The two were engaged to be married.

div.head: CRT FOR HHLP.
div.p: A CRT FOR HHLP.

The Coroner then had before him a witness named John Collins, who heard a cry for help on the night in question that must have come from one of the deceased —in his opinion from Miss Lowe. Collins, wlto is a carter, and lives in Bank-st., is employed by John Rathbone, lock-keeper at Hobby's Locks, and his testimony was to the effect that between eight and nine o'clock on Sunday evening he was going to the lock to attend to his horse. As he was crossing the field which separates the canal from Manchester-road he heard a scream and a cry for help. The sound was that of a woman's voice, and came front the direction of the swing bridge over the canal. He started running and, the night being very foggy, he Ptumbled over a sheep. It was so dark and foggy that it was difficult to find the way to the lock. When he reached the lock-house he procured a lamp, and went to the bridge, which he found partly open. Any person walking across and not know- ing that the bridge was open wenid step into the water. The bridge was about 8 feet wide. It was not always left as he found it; he believed some lads had been there. He found the umbrella produced. He looked along the water, but could see no signs of any person struggling. After searching with a boat hook, he went to the police station at Padgate and gave information of the occurrence. At half-past six the following morning he returned to the spat and then found the hat produced, which was float- ing in the lock. He was not present when the bodies were recovered. John Rathhone lived at the lock-house but no one had charge of the bridge. It was not a public bridge, but was for the convenience of the Canal Company and Mr. William Bennett, who farmed the land in the neighbourhood. The screams and shouts he heard proceeded, he had no doubt, from persons in the water. The Coroner : Not Horn anyone fighting on the bank ? Witness no, sir.—A juryman observed that the bridge would be open about five feet in the widest part.--The Coroner : if it had been light they could have got across without danger—Witness: Yes.—A .Juryman: I suppose on one is obliged to see that the bridge is closed ? Witness : No—A Juryman :It is very much used by the public on Sundays.—Another Juryman : But they are trespassing.
THE FINDING OF THE BODIES.

P.S. Barnes, stationed at Padgate, deposed to search- ing for the bodies on Monday morning, assisted by the lockkeeper. At 10.50 a.m., they, found the body of Hobert Barnett in the middle of the canal, about 30 yards from the bridge near the lock. His watch had stopped at nine o'clock. Ten minutes afterwards they, discovered the body of Edith Low two yards nearer the lock than where they found the other body. No signs of a struggle were evident. The bodies were removed to the Dog and Partridge. Witness bad the position of the bridge pointed out to him, and he was of opinion that anyone coming from the Cheshire side of the canal could not help walking int* the water.—A Juryman re- marked that the evidence of the sister had shown that they went in the direction of Latchford.—The Foreman: Then they would be coming along the feeder. _

NO MONT OF 'WAY. John Rathbone said that he lived on the canal side near Bobby's Lock. The canal belonged to the Ship Cana( Company. There was a swing bridge over the canal. There was no right of way over it; it was only an accommodation way for Air. Bennett. The boatmen passing through were not compelled to shut the bridge.

div.head: RESERVOIR DISASTER IN ARIZONA.
div.p: RESERVOIR DISASTER IN ARIZONA.

150 LIVES LOST. Navy Ironic, TUESDAY.—The courier, who has arrived at Phcenix Arizona, from the scene of the disaster at, Wickenburg, reports that a tremendous mountain of water descended from the flassa Yampa river, on Satur- day last, drowning thirty-one white men and three Chinese, who were working at the lower dam. Con- trary to the first accounts received, this courier states that Wickenburg is safe. The loss of life between Wickenburg and the dam is estimated at between thirty and forty.

NEW tmix, WEDNESDAY.—The "Herald" publishes a despatch from Plicenix, Arizona, stating that four couriers have arrived from the scene of the disaster at Prescott, bringing appalling accounts of the catasllroohe. It is now stated that fully:150 persons perished. Twenty. five bodies have been recovered. The surviving inhabi- tants are in a destitute condition. NEW YORK, WEDNESDAY EYENING.—From details now being received here regarding the Prescott disuster, it appears that twenty miles below the main deep dam of the reservoir was a smaller dam ma deep narrow canon being between them. The maiillikiam gave way at two o'clock, on Saturday morning, and an immense volume of water rushed down the gorge, sweeping everything before it, and lifting the smaller dam from its moorings. The flood, which is declared to have presented the ap- pearance of a wail of water forty feet high, reached Wick- enburg, in an hour, and completely destroyed the place. The bodies of six men Jou r women , and a child, i nhabi tante of Wickenburg. who fell victims to the disaster, have been found. Travelling onwards down the valley of the Hassagampa the water destroyed some structures at Seymour, a place some twelve miles off, where seven of the inhabitants are known to have perished. Three persons also lost their lives at Smith's Mills, four miles further on, while many intervening houses were demo- lished and their inmates drowned. In fact, from Smith's Mills to where the Hassagampa empties its waters into the Rio Giln, a distance of seventy-five miles, nearly every building in the valley was destroyed, and scarcely a building remains standing between the Giln and the main dam. The Mexican settlement at the junction of the two rivers was obliterated, twenty-one persons being drowned.

div.head: GREAT FIRE NEAR GREEN WICH.
div.p: GREAT FIRE NEAR GREEN WICH.

A report from Greenwich, states that at 12.15 a.m. on Sunday an explosion, followed by a ruinous fire, occurred at Forbes, Abbott, and Lennard's Chemical Works, Ordnance Wharf, Blackwell Point, resulting in the satire destruction of the premises, consisting of office, sheds, reservoirs, stills, &c. ; also two tank barges. The boiling pitch rolled over the wharf frontage in fiery cascades. The wind being easterly, carried the names across the draw dock to Edmond's Wharf, doing damage to the barge builders' shed, destroying one dozen empty barges aground on the foreshore. No persons were injured.
THE (MINES) EIGHT HOURS BILL

The following are the operative clauses of the Mines (Eight Hours) Bill A person shall not in any one day of 24 hours be employed underground in any Min. for a period exceeding eight hours from the time of his leaving the surface of the ground to the time of his ascent thereto, except in case of accident. Any em- ployer, or theagent of any employer, employing, or per- mitting to be employed, any person in contravention of this enactment, shall be liable to a penalty not exceed- iug 40s. for each offence, to be recovered in the same manner in which any penalty under the Acts relating to factories and workshops is recoverable." The Bill is backed by Mr. Philipps, Mr. C. Graham, Mr. Pickard, Mr. W. Abraham, Mr. Conybeare. Mr. Jacoby, Mr. Randall, Sir W. Foster, and Earl Compton.

div.head: – FUNERAL OF MR. BIGUAR, MX..
div.p: - FUNERAL OF MR. BIGUAR, MX..

The funeral of the late Mr. Biggar, M P., took place at Belfast: on Mon Flay. The procession started from St. Patrick's Church, Donegal-place, at about ten o'clock for the Carnnoney Churchyard. The coffin was covered with a mass of wreaths and crosses. The children of the Christian Brothers'School headed the procession, then came the Roman Catholic clergy, the hearse, Irish mem- bers of Parliament, Belfast merchants, and relatives. A very large crowd assembled along the route to testify their sympathy with deceased's friends and cplleagues. The visitors included 15 Irish members of Parliament. Mr. Parnell, who sent a wreath, was prevented from being present owing to indisposition. The Ratrfan Catholic clergy of Ulster attended in large,numhers, and the services at the.. grave were conducted by the Etishop ' I of the diocese.

The request was n.at granted, and the labourers quitted work. Subsequently the delegates called off the workers from several other vessels.

div.head: FATAL QUARREL AT STOCKTON.
div.p: FATAL QUARREL AT STOCKTON.

James Watson, a young labourer, belonging to Man- chester, quarrelled in a common lodging-house at Stock- ton, on Saturday niEtht, with a puddler, from Mother- well, named James Wilkie, because the latter had chaffed the former's paramour. Blows were exchanged, and Wilkie was heard to cry "Murder." Subsequently he was found in the street in an unconscious condition, and died soon afterwards. Watson has been arrested.

div.head: SWEATING COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE SWEATING COMMITTEE.

--- It is stated that the Sweating Committee have prac- tically rejected the report presented by its Chairman (the Earl of Dunraven), the majority of the members having voted for a report prepared by Lord Thring. The Chair- man is understood to have recommended what seem to have been regarded by the Committee as strong measures to prevent the evils complained of by means of increased inspeetion of workshops, the more stringent enforce. ment of the existing Factory Acts, and possibly restraint of pauper iminigrat ion.

div.head: O'SHEA DIVORCE CASE.
div.p: THE O'SHEA DIVORCE CASE.

The appeal of Mr. Tuohy, from the order of Justice Butt for payment of a fine of £lOO and costs imposed for contempt in connection with the publication of articles in the "Freeman's Jsurnal " respecting Captain O'Shea's , divorce case, was dismissed by the Appeal Court on Thursday, the Court taking the view that the appeal was from a writ which was equivalent to a summary conviction for a summary offence and that the Court, therefore, had no jurisdiction to hear it.

div.head: JUVENILE POISONER.
div.p: A JUVENILE POISONER.

At Chester. on Wednesday, Elizabeth Roberts, aged nine years, was charged with attempting to poison Annie Hodgkinson, a young woman, to whom her father, a widower, was engaged to be married. Miss Hodgkinson became violently sick on the 13th instant, and the child admitted having given her something. She said her grandmother told her to do it, but this the grandmother denied. It was stated that during the Maybrick trial the defendant took a great interest in the case. The defendant was ordered to be kept in a reformatory for seven years.

div.head: HORRIBLE TRAGEDY IN QUEBEC. MURDER OF A FAMILY. ESCAPE OF THE MURDERER.
div.p: HORRIBLE TRAGEDY IN QUEBEC. MURDER OF A FAMILY. ESCAPE OF THE MURDERER.

Navy YORK, MONDAY.—A man named Rodalphe Dubois, living at St Alban, Quebec, quarrelled yesterday, with his mother-in-law, and left his house for a time. He returned in a very excited state, haying drunk heavily, and killed the object of his hatred. He then turned up- on his family, and murdered his wife and two children. Sufficient time elapsed between the commission of the crime and its discovery to enable Dubois to escape, and though a number of townsmen have started in pursuit ho has not yet been caught.
CONFESSIONS OF A RUSSIAN EXILE.
PLOT TO ASSASSINATE THE CZAR.

Nsw YORK, TUESDAY.—A man named Pietchkejeff while repairing some electric works at Pierre, South Dakota, received a shock, and fell from a height of one hundred feet, fracturing both thighs. Believin that his end was near, • the man confessed that he was a Russian exile, and had been implicated in a plot in 1888 to assassinate the Czar by means of dynamite. fie also named several prominent Russian officials as having been likewise parties to the conspiracy, and declared that he had documents in his possession which would prove the truth of his statements.

div.head: TERRIBLE VOLCANIC ERUPTION.
div.p: TERRIBLE VOLCANIC ERUPTION.

Japanese mail advices which have just reached Queenstown give the details of one of the most terrible volcanic eruptions in the recent history of Japan. Mount Zoo, near the town of Fukuvama, in the Zing° district„ began to rumble at 8 o'clock on the evening of January 16. Soon the top of the mountain was lifted off. There was a din like a dynamite explosion, and sand and stones were belched forth. Stones and earth also fell at Mid- sunomimura, a village six miles sway. No previous eruption of Mount Zoo is recorded. Only one man lost his life, lout some cattle were killed and 55 houses were destroyed. The total loss entailed by the eruption is estimated at nearly 3,500,000 dols.

div.head: GERMAN ELECTIONS.
div.p: THE GERMAN ELECTIONS.

The results of about three hundred and fifty elections were known in Berlin on Sunday. The eartell majority is believed to have disappeared, and a great increase is observed in the nu.mber of votes obtained by the Social Democrats. A Berlin correspondent says that the repressive law against the Socialists, which is valid only till September,' is now doomed with the destruction of the eartell majority. TIT B SOSI.ALIST. PLATFORM.

The "Daily Chronicle gives the following as the Socialist platform circulated during the German electiens and subscribed by every Socialist candidate :—Universal military service, but militia instead of a, permanent Army; suppression of all laws against the fi•evdom of the Press and the right of public meeting and of association; universal education given by the State; a normal day of corresponding to the wants of society; prohibition f no child labour; unrestricted right of of kunday work the working classes to administer as they please funds raised for the relief of their comrades; and the substitu- tion of a single tax for all those at present in existence.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND:
div.p: STATE OF IRELAND:
EVICTIONS IN TIPPERARY.

Forty-five families, mostly shopkeepers in the town ot Tipperary, on the Smith-llarry property, have received notices of eviction, which are to be immediately en- forced. All the tenants concerned have removed their effects.

div.head: SHOCKING MURDER.
div.p: SHOCKING MURDER.

A Longford telegram states that information has been received there of the murder of a man name Cog, at Linacreeva., near Colehill. The skull of the deceased was smashed, and a Man has been arrested in connection with the crime. At the inquest, the jury returned an open verdict.

div.head: SENTENCE ON A PARISH PRIEST.
div.p: SENTENCE ON A PARISH PRIEST.

At Marylaorough, on Saturday, the hearing of a charge of illegal assembly against twenty persons, alleged to have endeavoured to erect huts on Clongorey estate commenced. Father Kinsella, one of the defendants, was convicted, and in default of sureties, was sent to gaol for two months. AN EDITOR'S CONVICTION QUASHED.

In the Exchequer Division, Dublin, on Wednesday, the Lord Chief. Baron and Mr. Justice Andrews quashed the conviction against Mr. Henry O'Connor, sub-editor of the " Leinster Leader," who was committed for publishing the reports of suppressed tranches of the National League. The court held that the evidence was insuffi- cient to connect the defendant with the publication. RENT REDUCTIONS 1N; TIPPERARY. . . .

The Land Commissioners for the.'n-11.;;7;f"fipperary delivered judgment, on Saturday, in cases recently heard before them, and made some very large reductions In the case of a farmer named Thompson his rent was reduced from £6OO to £470. Two tenants of Mr. Arthur Smith-Barry had the following reductions granted From £251 7s. to £2OO, and from £5O to £4O. INTEMPERANCE IN IRELAND. Bishop O'Dwyer, in his Lenten Pastoral, read on Sun- day, in the Limerick Diocese, referred at length to the increase of intemperance in Ireland, and called on the Roman Catholic clergy to use every effort to check the evil. The use of drinks at Irish wakes and funerals the Bishop denounced in unmeasured terms, and called on the clergy to put this almost national practice down with the greatest stringency. Were the Irish people temperate, he said, none would be better, for nearly all the poverty and misery of Ireland was attributable to the vice of Intem- perance.

TUE CASE OF O'DONNELL.

MR. SLATER LEWIS AND THE HOME SECRETARY. Mr. Slater Lewis, C.C., has had a long correspond- ence with Mr. Mathews, the Home Secretary, with regard to the case of Inspector O'Donnell, and other matters. We have not space for the whole of the letters, but give the last tsu—one from the Home @ffice, and Mr. Lewis's reply. They are as follows :

Whitehall, 7th February, 1890 Stn,—With reference to your letter of the 31st ultimo, and previous correspondence on the subject of the man- agement of the Cheshire constabulary, I am directed by the Secretary of State to inform you that he has made inquiry and has been in communication with the Chief Constable of the county on the various subjects men- tioned in your letter. With regard to the circumstances attending the resignation of Inspector O'Donnell. I am to point out that these involve a question of discipline, and thatthe Secretary of State has no powerto interfere with the decision of the Chief Constable in such a matter. The question of the fund alleged to have existed at Maccles- field for the reward of police officers securing the convic- tion of poachers appears to have been adequately dealt with by Colonel Hamersley. With regard to the allega- tions as to the improper employment of police constables in the place of gamekeepers, the Secretary of State finds on inquiry that in many particulars the information sup- plied to you is inaccurate, but in any case the matter is one that relates to the general control and management of the force, with which he cannot interfere, and can Only refer you to the Standing Joint Committee of the Quarter Sessions and County Council.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, E. LEIGH PEUBERTON. J. Slater Lewis, Esq., Stechford, nr. Birmingham. Stetchford, near Birmingham, 14th Fob., 1890 To the Right Hon. Henry Matthews. Q.C., M.P., Home Office, Whitehall, Leudon. Sir,-1 beg to acknowledge the receipt of your favour of the 7th inst., which leaves no doubt whatever in my mind that you have grasped at the shadow and missed the substance. You will pardon my using such an expression, but if you will kindly refer to the enclosure contained in my letter of the 23rd of December last, in which I make a series of charges against the police. you will see that your investigations do not appear to have taken cognizance of the whole of the incidents to which I drew public attention. You will observe (1) that I called attention to the most unsatisfactory state of affairs in regard to the Runcorn Police force, both in I resoect to drunkenness and to the whole of the police ' being drafted out of the town to watch for poachers at a point several miles away; and (2) that Colonel Hamersley had degraded Inspector O'Donnell and after- wards gave him a good conduct certificate. To the former of these two questions you do not refer, and the latteevou merely touch by saying you have no power to interfere. Now as the Treasury contributes one-half of the cost of the police force, and sends its inspectors round periodically to satisfy itself of the efficiency of the constabulary from national considerations, I should have thought it would have been of equal importance to know that the people in a town of 20,000 inhabitants, who, through the medium of local rates and the Treasury grant, contribute their full quota towards the cost of the police, have been deprived of that protection which is theirs by right and by law. As to your admission that you have no power to inter- fere with the chief constable in the matter of his first degrading O'Donnell and then granting him a good - conduct certificate, I can only say that such an admis- sion, coming from such a high quarter, is the best pos- sible proof that the law requires immediate alteration,for under the present system many innocent policemen who, like O'Donnell, have given the best years of their life in the service, have been cast adrift and thrown on the world without the slightest cause being assigned. But we look to the head of a police force for every- thing that is strictly legal and business like. We do not - expect them to issue certificates of good conduct to men who are unworthy of such certificates, and who may thus pass off as trustworthy persons into highly responsible positions for which they are not fit. I regret, too, that there is no answer to some very import- ant questions as to the behaviour of a superintendent of police, which it would have been, to say the least, satis- factory for us to have had. Nor is there any explanation why police constables should be told off to protect private grounds—such as Eaton Hall. This is distinctly against the law, unless such protection is paid for, which in this case it is not. When a few policemen were sent several years ago to protect the then Premier of England at Ha- warden, there were loud and angry protestations from certain quarters,but in this case the incident is winked at by those who are responsible for the administration of the law. If the Treasury pays one-half the cost of protect- ing private mansions and grounds, and the public the other half ( which after all means that we have to pay the lot) then I imagine that our rights are being most seriously infringed, and it is your duty on behalf of the British taxpayers to interfere. The publicans' sub- scription at New Brighton for new household furniture 'for the superintendent of the police is also not adverted to in your letter ; nor is the Knutsford case of gamekeepers and policemen playing into each others' kinds at the public expense, and while the houses in their respective beats were robbed of that protection for which the occupiers pay. Curiously enough you refer to "the funds alleged to have existed at Macclesfield for the reward of police officers securing the conviction of poachers." Now I never alleged anything of the kind as regards Macclesfield, which is not the point to which my statement had refer- ience. This instance of another fund existing for this scandalous purpose will clearly demonstrate the miserable despotism which has been reigning in the counties un- known to the outside world. When magistrates will stoop to offer a bribe to defeat the ends of justice, and possibly—nay probably have before them for punishment an innocent man, whose word is sworn down by cor- rupted policemen—what may we expect next! At any rate, I think the public are entitled toknow how Colonel Hamersley "adequately dealt "with such a gang. If every constable or other person connected with such a disgraceful intrigue were not immediately discharged they certainly should have been. Moreover the magis- trates themselves should have been struck off the list, as unworthy to occupy a seat on the bench. The last paragraph of your letter is no surprise to me. You come to a conclusion and deny the accuracy of my infor- mation without affording me the least opportunity of ,confirming the charges, which, I repeat, are substantally correct. In this same paragraph you state that" the employment of constables in the place of gamekeepers is a matter that relates to the general control and manage- ment of the force, with which you cannot interfere, and can only refer me to the Standing Joint Committee." I am sorry to say that the Standing Joint Committee is not composed of men (being as they are more than half magistrates) who will see full justice done in these matters, and to appeal to that tribunal would be nothing short of a perfect farce. I may say in conclusion that I undertook this onerous and disagreeable task solely as one of duty to the county, and I trust the correspond- ence, which I shall now hand to the press, may serve to show the public how their interests are neglected, and the welfare of their old servants in humble stations of life trampled underfoot—Apolog,ising for the length of this letter, I beg to remain, sir, your most obedient servant, J. SLAT= Lawns.

div.head: FRODSHAM GAS COMPANY.
div.p: FRODSHAM GAS COMPANY.

The annual meeting of the shareholders of this Company was held at the Gas Works on Thursday evening week. Dr. Robinson, the Chairman of the Board of Directors, presided. The Secretary, Mr. O'S. Frith, read the notice convening the meeting, and there was presented the report of the directors, which stated that on the firat of January, 1880, the -price of gas Was reduced from 48.7 d. to 4s. per 1.000 -cubic feet, and was continued at that rate although in October the price of coal supplied to the Com- pany was advanced Is. Bd. per ton. The revenue account showed a balance of £538 15s. 10i-d., out ot which the directors recommended the payment of a dividend of 10 per cent. The profit and loss account, after payment of the above, would have a balance of £709 1051. 41. to its credit. The directors had considered the question of a water supply to the dis- • triet, hut from the engineer's estimate of the cost of the required plant, there appeared to be no prospect of its paying and the directors had been reluctantly compelled to postpone the question. The directors recommended the issue of 50 210 shares, to raise the amount of floating capl al required for carrying on the business of the Company. The Chairman, after positing in review the Items of the balance sheet, proposed the adoption of the report, and the declaration of a dividend, pay- able on the Ist May, at the rate of 10 per cent. per annum, free from income tax. The motion was duly seconded. A shareholder asked if it were not possible to pay the dividend at an earlier date than that mentioned. The Chairman replied, that owing to the fact that the Company had no working capital, it would be inadvisable to do ; hut a resolution would be pro- posed to authorise the issne of fresh shares, so that they anight have a working capital, and the interest would be paid earlier in future years. The report was unanim- ously adopted. The auditors (Mr. W. Handley and Mr. T. D. Timmins) reported that the accounts were kept in a careful and orderly manner, and the books were in a very neat condition. Vouchers had been produced for all payments, and the secretary had always been in attendant:el on his duties whenever they had paid a visit to instrect the books.—lt was unanimously decided to give the directors power to issue 50 shares, of £lO each, either by public auction or by tender,. as they deemed best. The retiring directors, Dr. Robinson and Mr. J. W. Rothwell were re-elected ; and the retiring auditor Mr. W. Handley was also re-appointed, at the usual rate of remuneration.—ln answer to a question; the Chair- man said he war; glad to xplain that the sum of money owing by the late secretary had been satisfactorily made and provided for.—A vote of thanks to the directors, .„,and to the Chairman, concluded the proceedings.
