div.p: NORTH WICH DIVISION LIBERAL ASSOCIATION. ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual meeting of the members of this ,Asso- ciation was held at Gladstone Liberal Club, Northwich, on Saturday afternoon. There were representatives present from all parts of the divi- sion, those from Runcorn district being Messrs. T. Clegg, R. Moore, E. Wynne Humphreys, J. Clarke, Pickering. and H. Juke. Mr E. H. Moss, J.P., pre- sided, and explained that Mr. Brunner was on the continent and unable to attend the meeting. The Secretary (Mr. W. Handley, Runcorn), read his annual report as follows : —Twelve months ago this day our last annual meeting was held at Northwich, and though the report of our work as a political association for 1889 belongs rather to the quiet unobtrusive category (circumstances and the protracted session curtailed its otherwise aggressive character), we can point to pro- gress which we believe to be of a solid and substantial nature. (Hear, hear.) At our last annual meeting we adopted a resolution protesting against the pre- sent mode of governing our fellow subjects in Ireland, and though the people of Ireland, and many of its leaders were under a cloud of suspicion, owing to the violent death of District Inspector Martin, and the charges and allegations which were to be sub- mitted to the arbitrament of the Special Commission, we did not then, nor do we now, fear that an appeal to the constituencies would fully Justify such a resolution as that to which we gave so unanimous an expression. We also passed in review, led by our staunch friend the Rev. F. Minton, M.A., those many and needful reforms known as the platform of the National Liberal Federation. Mr. Minion's speech on that occasion proved how intensely he sympathises in those questions which affect the social well-being and moral elevation of the larger masses of our fellow-men, and of which he has evinced such a masterly grasp in his recently published books" Capital aind Wages" and "The Welfare of the Millions." At our ex- ecutive meeting,held shortly after wards,the usual arrange- ments were made for actively continuing the work of re- gistration which, after all, is the main factor in every political contest, as inattention to its demands has led either to defeat or non success in several constituences, where the highly strung conditionof political feeling gave a confident expects.tion of victory,at the poll. The work of registration was earnestly undertaken by your agents, and when the Revising Barrister had concluded his work we could point to the following as the secured result :
.... . Owners claims allowed Liberals 35 Tory 22 Occupiers „ „ Of 263 go 85 OW and new lodgers 94 89 ~ ~
392 206 Struck off on Objection „ 45 • 62

347 Net Liberal gain on reviaing, 203. A suggestion thrown out at our last annual meeting of having a divisional excursion to Hawarden, was con- sidered and adopted by the executive, and the trip took place on Whit Tuesday and though our chief was absent from home, doing the party yeoman service in Cornwall, several hundreds of our electors and friends availed themselves of the opportunity of visiting his house and 'greatly enjoyed themselves. Mr. Brunner and Mr. Ellis accompanied the excursionists. The next executive meeting was convened on the requisition of three of its members, the special business being to con- sider the suggested presentation of an address to Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone on their golden wedding day. It is almost needless to state that the suggestion was approved and a suitable address prepared both in matter and form by our hon. sec. The address was a fine specimen of the engrosser's art, and by arrangement was presented on behalf of the Association through Mr. Brunner. Liberal progress has during the year been un- mistakeably proved by the opening of a Liberal Institute at Halton, a Liberal Club at Runcorn, and the erec- tion of the Gladstone Club, Northwich, which from its imposing appearance and wealth of accommodation may be fitly styled the National Liberal Club of the Northwich Division. In addition to these tangible signs of progress there is projected the erection of a new club at Winsford, the infusion of renewed energy in the existing slob at Davenham and Barnton, and if these valuable agen- cies are managed by steadily keeping in view the three- fold object of recreation, reading, and political instruction the existence of so many clubs in our division must be an important factor in the political education of the constituency. The report also referred to the death of Mr. J)seph Slater, the chairman of the Winsford district, at the ripe age of 83, and to the removal to another division of Mr. John Thompson. Two matters, the report continued, though somewhat outside our direct work as an association, may be approprietely mentioned in, connection therewith. The County Council in May-last, on the motion of Mr. Killick— whom at our last annual meeting we had the pleasure of congratulating by telegram on his election the day previously as County Councillor—appointed a Committee to enquire apd report as to the'need for alter- ation in the polling districts, polling places, and the holding of Revision Courts, and your secretary at once drew up a scheme embodying such alterations as local experience had proved desirable. This -repert was sub- mitted to and approved by our honorary secretary and also to our agents in the district affected thereby and was approved by them; it was also submitted to the Conservative agent, Mr. Hughes, and by arrangement Mr. Hughes and myself attended the the polling district committee w: ich was held at Northwich on June 12th consisting of Messrs. Moss, Speakman, Kay, and France- Hayhurst. and presented it as a joint report, and unanimously accepted by the Committee, it was adopted by the County Council at their next meeting. North- wich is now divided into two polling districts of Castle and Witten; Middlewich polling district is added to by the inclusion of the township of Clive; and Over and Wharton polling districts are united under the name of the Winsford polling district. At the subsequent revision these alterations materially assisted the con- venience of the Revising Barrister and the townships concerned. At the invitation of Mr. leillick; representa- tives from several of the Paniamentary divisions of Cheshire attended a meeting at Crewe, on August 3rd, our Association being represented by Mn. Brunner, Mr. Moss, Mr. Fletcher and your secretary ; and as the result, the Cheshire Liberal Federal Council was formed, its object being the promotion of Liberal interests in the County of Chester. From the fact that the County Council electoral areas are entirely distinct from, and in most cases overlap the Parliamentary Divisions, the necessity for such a Federation at a time of election can- not be doubted and it may become an important factor in County Council elections if the associations decide to conduct them on party lines. As one result already of its existence, the County Council have, on its application agreed that in the urban districts the register shall in future be made out in street form, so far as is possible under existing local circumstances. The last annual ' meeting found us eager and ready for the hard work of an election, this year brings us nearer to that desirable day, but in our tancied security we must not lightly estimate the forces arrayed against us ; not only, are we to have the army in front, with whom we have afore- time successfully grappled, but we are threatened with an organised flank movement, backed by powerful in- fluence and great wealth, having. its origin, and prob- ably its centre, in our own division, but if we keep united, enthusiastic, full of noble and resolute ardour, sustained by the remembrance of the magnificent result, achieved in our lastcontest, defeat is impossible; and we shall have the honour of taking part in the'comine struggle which must sweep on ,with a steady and irresis- tible purpose towards that great consummation of national justice and reconciliation width, will crown the august life of our revered leader, Mr. W. E. Gladstone, and which will redound more than all the glory of battle fields to the greatness, stability, and renown of England" —(Applause).—The report was unanimously adopted. Mr. Fletcher proposed that Mr. E. H. Mossbe re-elected president, arid remarked that Mr. Moss had done great service in the cause of Liberalism, and as president had the full confidence of every member. (Applause.)—Mr. G. E. King seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously.—The following CAMS were also re- appointed :—Mr. G. H. Deakin, chairman of council ; Mr. H. Brett, C.C., chairman of executive; Mr. E. Milner, hon. treasurer ; and Mr. A. Fletcher, hon. sec.— Mr. Fletcher said he was glad to do all he could for the Association. hut the work of the hon. sec. was lightened to an almost inappreciable degree by the efficient services of the paid secretary. (Hear, hear.) Twelve co-opta- tive members of the council were chosen, and the follow- ing 13 gentlemen were selected to represent the Associa- tion at the National Liberal Federation :—Messrs. G. H. Deakin' H. Brett. C.C., A. Fletcher, Rev. F. Carter, H. Capes, W. Molvneux, T. Handle', W. Ockleston, J. Millineton, W. Handley, P. Speakman, E. H. Moss, J.P., James Handley, J.P.—Messrs. Moss, Fletcher. and Ockleston were appointed representatives on the Cheshire Liberal Federal Council. Mr. Milner read thefinancial statement, which showed the Association was in a better position than in former years, but the treasurer appealed to the member to pay their subscriptions before the end of the year.—On the proposition of Mr. Wynne Flumphreys, seconded by Mr. T. Clege, the report was adopted. Mr. W. Hough proposed, "That this representative Council of the Northwich Divisien Liberal Association cordially welcomes their esteemed member on his return from a prolonged absence in improved health, rejoices with him in the recovery of his son Mr. Sidney Brunner from a serious illness, thanks him for his parliamenta7 services and trifsts that he may long represent this Divi- sion in the Imperial Parliament." Mr. T. Clegg seconded the motion which was carried unanimously. Mr. Fletcher then proposed "That the Council of this Association sympathise with their friend Mr. T. E. Ellis, M.P., in his illness and enforced absence from home, and hopes he will be speedily restored to sound health and increased usefulness in the service of his country."—The Rev. F. Carter seconded the proposi- tion, which, was carried by acclamation. Mr. E. Milner 'proposed the adoption of an extensive proeramine of Liberal reform, and Mr. E. Wynne Hum- phreys seconded the resolution, which was adopted. A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the pro- ceedings.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN.
"BY AN OCCASIONAL COBILBSPONDENT."

That the meeting of the Noithwich Division Liberal Association,on Saturday.was shorn of much of its interest through the enforced absence of Mr. Brunner on the continent, but there was, nevertheless, an earnest and successful gathering of delegates.

That a strong desire for an early dissolution was evinced, in the belief that a, great Liberal victory would result throughout the country, and with the local register in the most perfect condition possible, no fear is felt of the trriumphant return of Mr. Brunner. That the Executive Committee of the Conserva- tive Association have held a meeting during the week, with a view of preparing for a general elec- tion, and, reading between the lines, it would ap- pear that Mr. Brunner's opponent on the next occa- sion will be a Conservative and not a Liberal- Unionist, as many have supposed would be the case. As the Unionists in the Division might he counted on the fingers of both hands, this course is perhaps the wisest, but if the Liberal party work with the eaergy and determination that characterised their operations at the last contest, the Tory nominee will have a crushing repulse. That for many years past the advantair-, and nee- cessity of connecting Halton-road district.with New- town, has been observed, but the idea of con4truct- ing such a road was allowed to remain dormant That it is probable the thoroughfare will now be made. The Ship Canal Company have signified their willingness to construct a bridge over the Big Pool, and Major Orred has consented to give the necesiary land from that point to Oreenway-road, Board School: It is estimated that the cost of making the road will be about .£1,500, and Major Orred. it is understood, has offered to contribute £l,OOO towards that amount.
• That the town will thus secure a splendid and convenient road for the sum of £5OO.

That the emissions of noxious vapours from the Runcorn Works of the Sow and Alkali Company are becoming more frequent and iaore pungent in their odour. The nuisance is bad enotigh to those who have to pass the works daily, but to those persons who live at the lower end of Greenway-road, it must be almost unbearable.

That one morning, about a week ago, the gases sent forth penetrated into High-st., and greatly hin- dered the tradesmen in the conduct of their busi- ness. A complaint was made to the Nutsance Inspector, who conveyed the complaint to the works.
That it is to be hoped the Inspector ha § brought the matter under the notice of the Health Coin- mittee, and that the Board of Commissioners will take the subject in hand.

That there have been numerous applications for the post of Surveyor to Widnes Local Board, which will proceed to make the appointment on Monday next, in spite of the protest of "infliential inhabi- tants" against the dismissal of Mr. Higginson. That Mr. Hugh O'Donnell, fornerly inspector of police at Runcorn, and who now resides at Widnes, was one of the 400 applicants for a road inspector- ship under the Cheshire County Council, but, as the list of tht• appointments made public shows, he was unsuccessful.

That the proposed recital of the opera" Mar itana," by the members of Runcorn Musical Society, has been abandoned for the present season because of the inability to secure efficient principals. In tead, a ballad concert will be given.
THE IMPRISONED FRENCH PRINCE.

A Paris telegram says the fear of a Ministerial, and even a Presidential, crisis has decided the Government in abandoning their original intention of pardoning the Duc d'Orleans. It seems certain now that the young Prince will be obliged to undergo at least a part of his sentence, most probably in the prison of Clairvaux. For the present, however, he remains at the Conciergerie, where he still continues to receive visits from the Duchesse de Chartres, Princess Marguerite, the Duc de Luynes, and M. Bother. A " Herald " telegram says the Duc d'Orleans was on Monday transferred to Clairvaux Prison. He was taken from the Conciergerie an hour before the starting of the train. The fact of his departure is being kept a pro- found secret.

div.head: ELECTION INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: ELECTION INTELLIGENCE.
GREENOCK.

_ Mr. Cuninghame Graham, M.P., has announced hi Intention of contesting Greenock at the next election as a representative of the Labour party. CAVAN (WEST). The name of Mr. Knox, an Ulster Protestant and Home Ruler, member of the Eighty Club, and an Oxford graduate, is being mentioned in connection with the vacancy. STAMFORD.
The nomination of candidates for the Parliamentary vacancy in the Stamford division of Lincolnshire is fixed fdr Monday next, and the pollirig for Friday week, the 7th of March.

NORTH MONMOUTHSHIRE. Captain T. P. Price, M.P., the Gladstonian member for North Monmouthshire, has intimated to the Liberal Association of the division that he will not offer himself for re-election at the next general election. Captain Price has represented the division since 1885. WATERFORD (WES I') ELECTION. The nomination took place at Dungarvan, on Monday, of a candidate to fill the vacancy in the representation of the West Division of Waterford County, caused by the presumed death of Mr. Jasper Douglas Pyne. Mr. Alfred Webb, a Nationalist and a member of the Society of Friends, of Dublin was the only candidate nominated, and he was declared du.y elected. Mr. Webb is a printer, and lives at Lismaben," Dartrey Park, Rathmines, Dublin.

div.head: DEAN LEFROY HITS HARD.
div.p: DEAN LEFROY HITS HARD.

Seldom has a more plain spoken sermon been delivered in a Royal chapel than that preached by the Dean of Norwich, on Sunday morning, at the Chapel Royal, Whitehall. Dr. Lefroy, (formerly Archdeacon of Warrington) chose for his text Ezekiel xxii. 14, "Can thine heart endure or thine ; hands be strong in the days when I shall deal with thee?" He riveted the attention of the cengrega- tion while he drew a striking parallel between the state of Judah and of England. Agin the prophet's time in Judah, so in England now—disobedience to , parents, fraud in business, degradation of politics, and the COrpses of the dead faith were to he endountered on every side. Men and women in I society treated the violation of the seventh corn- ' mandment as a mere bagatelle. The lack of serious- ness of mind was one of the saddest signs of the times. Men and women. reckless and penniless, ' who see the frivolous way ih which those who have ' no care or anxiety, and who always walk on the ! sunny side of the street, waste their lives. curse and loathe the grandeur that mocks poverty. Men on exchanges and marts, and who form corners for ; their own aggrandisement, so adroitly conduct their ; business as to keep within the law,but equally with , the butterflies of fashion who flit from flower to I flower, they resist the expostulation,of God, and act with a selfish frivolity which must, if persisted in, ; bring down God'a curse on the Church and realm of England.

div.head: 'DROWNING OF .TWO LOVERS.
div.p: THE 'DROWNING OF .TWO LOVERS.
FUNERAL YFATERDAY.

Yesterday afternoon the bodies of Robert Barnett end Edith Lowe, who were drowned on Sunday night under circumstances reported on another page, were interred at the Cemetery in the presence of a large concourse of people. A portion of the funeral procession left the late residence of Barnett, in Buttermarket-at., soon after two o'clock, and as it proceeded through Church-st. it was joined by a second hearse containing the remains of the young woman, who lived in Greenell-st., and by a number of coaches in which wer seated the relatives and friends of Miss Lowe. The two portions then formed into one long procession, and its passage along the route to the cemetery was witnessed by crowds of people. A large crowd also assembled in the Cemetery, where the two coffins, which were made exactly alike, were lowered into the same grave. They were covered with wreaths that, had been sent by sympathising friends. The Rector (the Rev. F. W. Willis) officiated at the graveside, and also conducted a service in the Church of England building. The bodies were interl•ed in Protestant ground, but, as one of the decea4ed. Barnett, was a Roman Catholic, a service Recording to the Catholic religion was conducted, on Thursday, at the 110lISP where he had resided. The funeral arrangements were superintended by Mr. Lowden Wells, under- taker, Foundry-st. Amonstthewrpaths forwarded was a very handsome one from a number of the girls employed at Cockedge factory, bearing the inscrip- tion "'ln loving memory;" one from the Rector and Mrs Willis; and one from the fellow-workmen of Barnett.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 1, 1890. THE SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 1, 1890. THE SHIP CANAL.

RUNCORN MISSION. The second anniversary of the Ship Canal mission at Runcorn was celebrated, on Sunday, when special sermons were preached, in the morning by Mr. John Watson, the missioner, in the Ovening by the Hon. wad Rev. F. Grimston, M.A., there being large congregations at each service. On Monday evening a tea and public meeting was held, the ladies presiding at the tables being Mesdames Watson, Foster, King, Ashford, Lewis. Davies, Graham, and Free, and the Misses Foster, Ashford, Rutter and Percival. After tea Mr. C. A. F. Gregson occupied the chair, and delivered a short address, and speeches were also made by the Hon. and Rev. R. Grimston, and Messrs. Livesley and Wilson, whilst Mr. J. Watson des- cribed the work accomplished during the past year. The proceedings were enlivened during the evening by solos, which were given in a pleasing manner by Mrs. Watson and Miss Forster, and a glee, "Laughing chorus," which was rendered by friends of the mission. On Tues- day evening a service of song, entitled "Tom o' Jack's Lad" was given in a successful manner by the choir, assisted by friends, Mr. J. Brow, being the reader. There was a large and appreciative audience, and the chair was occupied by Mr. Cullis. SHIP CANAL MISSION, STOCKTON HEATH. An entertainment in connection With the Band of Hope was given, on Tuesday. in the above room, which was crowded. After a suitable address by the Chair- man, Mr Taylor, the resident missionary, an excellent pr9gramme was gone through, recitations being given by the following :—Miss V. Beswick, D. James, P. Travis, M. Dodds, E. Churchill, R. Hughes N. Dodds, S. Risley, A. Gregory, Master G. Robin, and J. Robin; a violin solo by Master T. Hughes; a Lancashire sketch by Mr. Hallows. Several songs and melodies were also given at intervals. A most enjoyable evening was brought to a close by a humourous domestic scene entitled "Rum and Tea," given by the following 4—Miss Perrin, Miss Robin, Miss Risley, Miss Reid, Miss Moses, Miss Beswick, Miss Hallows, and Mr. Hallows.

div.head: AMERICA.
div.p: AMERICA.
WARRINOTONIANS IN NORTH-WEST
LETTER PROM MR. JAMES WINSTANLEY.
We give below an interesting letter, dated February 9ch, whin Mr. John Gandy, of this town, has just received from Mr. James Winstanley, formerly sf Warrington, but now living in Salem, Oregon.

div.head: NO MAILS. "LA GRIPPE "IN THE NORTH-WEST.
div.p: NO MAILS. "LA GRIPPE "IN THE NORTH-WEST.

I have, wrote Mr. 'Winstanley, not received a letter since I wrote your last. There has been no mail received in Salem for nearly three weeks, all communications with ,the world outside of the valley having been cut off by either snow or water. The past two weeks have been as eventful as any in my life. In the first place I want to tell of a German family who reside on the next ranch but one north of us, by name Kurtz. They had a son 22 years of age, as fine a young man as you ever saw; he stood over six feet, and quite as stout as you. He had "la grippe" and it left him with lung fever, and he only lived five days. Mrs. Winstanley was with him two days, and I sat up with him the last night of his life. Truly it was very sad, but he died trusting in the Saviour. They are a good family, opening the day with family prayer, and closing with the same. This son passed his "exam." at Salem College, where he was a student only two weeks ago. I put the poor fellow in his coffin. Twenty carriages followed him to the Cemetery.

div.head: RAINS AND FLOODS.
div.p: RAINS AND FLOODS.

. It rained incessantly for with the following result—the rain melted the snow in the mountains and the river began to rise. I drove to town a week ago last Friday, and found the bridges floating and the roads impassable ; after that tile river began to overflow its banks, and, though generally about a quarter of a mile wide, it now got to be thr'e miles wide, spreading well over in Polk County. We live in Marion County; bye- and-bye people on our ;tide of the river began to get scared, and last Monday morning it was just running over the road in the lowest places. Before night, houses, bridges, granaries, came floating down. Hundreds of sawn logs, cut in the hills for the timber mills, and large trees seven, eight, and even nine feet through, came floating down, torn up by the roots with the violence of the rushing, surging water. Some curious animals came floating down on the drift; among others a cougar howl- ing on a log. Some shots were fired at him, but they did not kill him. Horses, cows, hogs, chickens by the hun- dreds, have been drowned.

div.head: FLOODED 0177.
div.p: FLOODED 0177.

On Monday night I took the precaution to lead out my horses and cows from the barn (which stands rather low) on to a hill aco.ss the road, it being the highest part of my ranch. I thus saved their lives. Tuesday morning at three o'clock we were roused up by the rushing of water round and under the house, which is a wooden structure and stands on oak logs, about 18 inches high. I remembered my hogs were fast in the stye, so I waded out to them and let them out. I began to fear they would drown, but I finally got them in the wood shed, and got a lot of firewood down for them to scramble on. In the house we began to take up the carpet and every- thing movable upstairs. I pumped a lot of water out of the well before the river got to it, and got a lot of dry firewood in, and packed all our food flour and sugar up- stairs. We waited and watched the dreadful water rise , inch by inch until it got level with the verandah floor, and then from across the water we saw two men on horseback coming to rescue us. They waded their horses through the flood : we hoisted our piano on a table and left the house to its fate, having anchored it to a tree I which grows at the back door. We bade good-bye to our homestead with sad and anxious hearts, and the two brave German boys ferried Us to the hill, on the backs of their horses, and here let me say that I never saw two men work harder or more bravely than these two young men. In the next house sciath there was a family in a worse fix than us. They had no upstairs, and the house was considerably lower than ours. The man who rented the place, a Mr. Warren, and wife and two children, Mr. Warren's mother and father living along with them to take care of their daughter; who is a cripple, being paralysed with rheumatism. The two young men got some fir poles and made a raft in the water, one standing in the water while the other fas- tened them together. They then tore some of the doors from the house and got the poor cripple in a chair on the raft, with her husband to help to steady her. They towed the raft to the knoll, where I had a waggon wait- ing, and we lifted her and chair in the waggon and hauled her through the woods to a house that stood high and dry. Meanwhile the young men tried te make another trip to the house to rescue the old people and children, but they could not get the raft along against the current, which ran too strong for the horses to haul against. However, they moored it to a tree, and packed the old peonle on the horses, and finally got them all to land. While all this was being done, some Oregonions who lived just across the way, high and dry, would not so much as lend a hand to save the poor pemple. They would have done it sharp enough if there had been twenty or thirty dollars at the end of the job. They are the meanest men in creation: it is all self with them all through. Well, sir, these Germans took us to their homes and housed and fed us with great kindness. The water continued to rise, the water in the orchard being twelve or fourteen feet deep, and it only needed five feet more to drive us from there. All hands pre- pared for the worst ; all the outhouses were fastened down, and horses and cows driven to the woods, and your humble servant built a boat with no other tool than a woodman's axe and a bucksaw and hammer; a primitive affair it is, I can tell you just to carry the women and children across to the woods, our only hope of safety. But we did net need it.

THE WATERS SUBSTDE. On Wednesday morning, the water began to subside, and it sank about one inch per hour. Towards night I canght my hoise and swam it across to the house to see if my hogs were alive: They were all right, as also were the chickens. I fed them all and went back to , sleep. Party next morning something' impressed me I should go home. I started at daylight, and when I got there I found I was not the first. There was a matt with an axe in his hand, and his boy, in the hen house. I quietly asked him his business, and he said he had come to see if the chickens were all alive; but I guess they would not all have lived long if I had not come on the scene.. After washing some of the mud nut of the house, I got a waggon to fetch home my family.. Just as I started to go, two men came along on horse-back from town, and seeing my bee hives washed in the fence, they helped themselves to the honey. I asked them not to take it as it belonged to me, but they said all the same they would. Both they and the man in the hen house were Oregouions. I told them they shot such men as , them at the Johnstown flood—that was all they were worth. I find I have only lost about half a mile of fence, and my bees, and about an acre and half of land. • There are many, a little way down, who have lost all they had-- house and barn awl all stock and fences. It is simply starting afresh. What was a little while ago fine farms with grain growing and fenees all round are now , com- plete wrecks. The family I stayed with lost over two miles of fence. lam thankful to say Ido not hear of any lives being loot as yet. I believe a train a little way below Portland—that is about 60 miles from here—was wrecked and 16 lives lost. It is 29 years since there was a flood like this in Salem. The bridge across the Wiliamitee is washed away, and many thousand dollars worth of damage done. lam thankful to say we are all well.

Lord Harris, with Lady Harris and suite, left London dn Tiorrsday morning for Bombay!, to take up his new riuties as Governor of the Province, in succession to Lord Reny. The Liverpool pilot boat No 8 was sunk, off Point Lynas, having been in collision with the screw steamer Ilydal Water. Mr. James Atherton, the pilot captain, was thrown into the water, and was rescued with con- siderable difficulty.

MARRIAGE OF A RUNCORN TRADESMAN'S SON, At the Parish Church of Weaverham, on Tuesday, the marriage of Mr. William Gittins, jun., of Run- corn, and Miss Nellie Bean, daughter of Mr. Wm. Bean, Island Farm, Dutton, was solemnzied, the ceremony being performed by the Rev. T. E. Scott. The bride, who was given away by her father, was attired in a dress of pale blue cashmere, trimmed with white swansdown and orange blossoms, with hat to match of pone silk and white ribbon. The brides- maids were Miss Gittins, Mias Bean, who wore dresses of fawn cashmere trimmed with plush, with hats to match, and Miss Lucy Bean and Miss Bettie Bean, who wore cream muslin dresses, with old gold pongee silk sashes and cream hats to match. Each of the brides- maids carried a basket of flowers. Mr. John Peck officiated as best man, and after the ceremony breakfast was partaken of, and the happy couple left Dutton for Southport. The presents were numerous, the bridegroom being the recipient of a splendid marble timepiece, the gift of the men employed at the Atlas Chemical Com- pany, Widnes ; also a piano, which was given by his father, Mr. William Gittins.

THE CHESS CONTEST.

The twelfth and final game of chess at Liverpool, was played yesterday, and resulted in Lesker, the German champion, beating Bird, the Englishman, by seven to two. There were three draws. MINERS ON THE EIGHT HOURS' MOVEMENT.

Yesterday a ballotoFiWNortimmbeiCand miners on the eight hours' question resulted in a unanimous deci- sion against the proposal, and, like the ruiners of Dur- ham, they are opposed to legislative interference.

_ • LIBEL ACTION BY MR. MICHAEL DAVITT. The "Freeman's Journal" of yesterday says :—" We understand that Mr. Michael Davitt has commeAced pro- ceedings against the ' Spectator ' for libel contained in statements connecting him with the Manchester sescue."

THE REPRESENTATION OF STOKE-ON-TRENT. Mr. George Leveson Gower, Liberal candidate for Stoke-upon-Trent, issued his address on Friday. He advocates Home Rule for Ireland, one man one vote, disestablishment of the Welsh Church, and abolition of school fees. The Conservative candidate will probably be Mr. Shepherd Allen. THE EXTRAORDINARY STORY OF TEL-EL- KEBIR.

John Sandilands writes to Friday's "Glasgow Mail" contradicting Corporal Palmer's statement in the "Nine- teenth Century" that two Glasgow Irishmen were shot as traitors during the battle of Tel-El-Bebir. Sandilands was in Palmer's regiment, and says only two Glasgow men were killed by the enemy—Paterson and Pollock.

div.head: RAILWAY ACCIDENT IN IRELAND.
div.p: RAILWAY ACCIDENT IN IRELAND.

About four o'clock yesterday morning, a goods train from Waterford dashed into several coal wagons lying at the Cahir station of the Waterford and Limerick Rail- way. Some empty trucks next to the engine were smashed, but the latter was not damaged. Neither the driver nor the fireman was injured. The passenger traffic was delayed for a time.

div.head: LETTER FROM MR. GLADSTONE.
div.p: LETTER FROM MR. GLADSTONE.

Mr. Gladstone, writing to Mr. Bolton, says that the placing of the Irish question in the forefront of the battle suffices to secure the right hon. gentleman's warmest wishes for his return. The efficiency of Parliament depended on that question, and he urgently advised that, for British ends, the Irish question should be settled. He hoped, also, that North St. Pancras, by returning Mr. Bolton, would express constitutionally their indignation at the monstrous calumnies and forgeries by which it had been attempted ta crush the hopes of Ireland through ruining the character of her members and their leader.

div.head: NORTH ST. PANCRAS ELECTION.
div.p: THE NORTH ST. PANCRAS ELECTION.

The nominations of candidates for the vacancy in North St. Pancras were received by the returning officer between 10 and 12 o'clock yesterday morning. The nomination papers of Mr. Thomas Henry Bolton (Glad- stonian Liberal) and Mr. Harry R. Graham (Conserva- tive) were handed in at ten o'clock. Mr. John Leighton (Independent Unionist) afterwards handed in his nomi- nation papers. There are thus three candidates going to the poll. At five minutes past 12 Mr. John Leighton applied to withdraw his nomination paper, but as the time had expired the returning officer refused fo Permit the withdrawal.

div.head: SIR MORELL MACKENZIE'S LIBEL ACTION,
div.p: SIR MORELL MACKENZIE'S LIBEL ACTION,

The action by Sir Morell Mackenzie against Mr. Edward Steinkpoff, proprietor of the "St. James's Gazette," for libel, in stating in letters to Mr. Greenwood, former editor ot the " St. ja.mes'e Gazette," that Sir Morell had made mistakes in his treatment of the Emperor Frederick, and that he had been charged with con- spiracy by concealing the fact of the disease being cancerous to secure the Emperor's succession, was tried in the Queen's Bench division on Friday. The jury found a verdict tor the plaintiff, with £1,500 damages Sir Morell Mackenzie's action against the " Times "was then called, and in this a verdict by consent for £l5O, and taxed costs, was taken.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.-FRIDAY.

The House met at a quarter past four. The Earl of WEMYSS drew attention to the evils of over examining for examination, and moved the appointment of a Royal Commission to inquire into and report on the whole subject, and to collect information bearing on the matter from other countries. Lord Cranbrook and Earl Granville opposed the motion, which was withdrawn. The House then adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.

The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. THE NtW MAGAZINE RIFLE.—The Secretary for war, replying to General Grossman, said that the new maga- zine rifle was a composite rifle. PROPOSED ADJOURNMENT.—Mr. BUCHANAN asked leave to move the adjournment, as the Government's action in changing the form of submitting the estimates limited debate, but the Speaker said the question should be raised by moving progress in Committee of Supply. The question dropped temporarily,, but the House hav- ing gone into Committee Mr. Bnchanan proceeded to raise the question again. He eventually withdrew the motion.

THE CLEVELAND-ST. SCANDALS.—MY. LABOUCHERE moved a resolution to call attention to the action of cer tam n officials in confederation to defeat the ends of justice, by allowing the man Hammond to escape from the country after the exposure of the Cleveland-street scandals. He declared that a sentence of nine months on the pseudo-clergyman was totally and scandalously inadequate, (Cheers.) and charged the Government with trying to hush up the scandals. Be highly corn. mended the action of the Prince of Wales in endeavour- ing to have justice done. The police and post office top had also done their duty. The whole blame rested with the Treasury. He contended that the proper steps had not been made to get the man Hammond from Belgium or France; and he charged the Government with inter- fering with the police to prevent the arrest of Lord Arthur Somerset. Poormen, he said, had been sent to prison while rich men had been allowed to escape. He charged Lord Salisbury with having conveyed informa- tion to a friend that a warrant was to be issued, and thus enabled Lord Somerset to getaway. He knew other persons who ought to be arrested, bat, through some powerful influence, that had not been done. Be con- cluded by saying he distinctly charged Lord Salisbury and others with a criminal conspiracy to defeat the ends of justice and he asked for a. Committee to inquire into charges and allegations.—The Arroassi-Gassm, in Indignant terms, repudiated the charges. He challenged Mr. Labouehere to give the authority on which he made the charge. Mr. Lemma/sax declined to give the name, (loud Ministerial cheers), but he said : 1 will write it on a bit of paper, and then the Attorney-Generel could so announce it if he liked. (Loud Oppositi -11 Cheers). The ATTORNEY-GENERAL then proceeded wi 's speech, and said that when Lord Salisbury met Deighton Pro. bin, he, Lord Salisbury, distinctly dented that he had ever mentioned that a warrant was to be issued.

div.head: MR. LABOUCHERE StTSPENDED.
div.p: MR. LABOUCHERE StTSPENDED.

A later telegram says—Mr. Labaucheve has just been suspended for declaring that he did not believe Lord Salisbury and refusing to withdraw the expression. The hon. member withdrew from the House, declaring that he regretted his conscience would not allow him to be- lieve Lord ,Salisbury.

IMBECILE PATLIANTS.—Mr. aliddielaurst drew attention to the fact the they had recently had a large increase in the number of imbecile inmates. IN PARLIAMENT, SESSION 1690. WARRINGTON EXTENSION WATER AND IMPROVEMENT BILL. ' I DO HEREBY GIVE NOTICE, that at the PUBLIC MEETING of the Owners and Ratepayers of the Borough of Warrington, held on Friday. the 21st day of February. 1890, at the Public Hall, Rylands-street, pursuant to the pro- visions of an Act of-the 35th and 36th Victoria, Chapter 91, intituled "An Act to authorise the application of Funds of Municipal Corporations, and other governing bodies in certain cases," it was resolved that such Meeting be adjourned to Menday. the Third day of March next, AND I DO HEREBY GIVE NOTICE that such ADJOURNED MEETING will be held accordingly, at the CO-OPERATIVE HALL, CAIRO-STREET, ON MONDAY NEXT, THE THIRD DAY OF MARCH, 1890, AT HALF-PAST SEVEN O'CLOCK IN THE AFTERNOON. Dated this '2sth day of February. 1890. RICHARD WALKER FRANCOMB. •Mayor.

IN PARLIAMENT—SESSION 1890. IU-ANCHESTER SHIP CANAL (TIDAL OPEN- III &C.) BILLS AND WIDNES BRINE SUPPLY BILL. At a MEETING of the owners and ratepayors of the district of Widnes held at the Board-room, Town Hall, Widnes, pursuant to the Act 35 and 36 Vic., c. 91, this Fourth Feb., 1890, the above-named Bills were considered and thefollowing resolutions passed, viz. : Resolved, that this meeting of owners and ratepayers of the district of Widnes, in the county of Lancaster, do consent to the opposition by the Local Board for the said district, to a Bill now pending in Parliament. intituled, "A Bill to alter certain works authorized by the Manchester Ship Canal Act, 1885; and for other purposes." Resolved, that this meeting of owners and ratepayers of the district of Widnes, in the county of Lancaster, do consent to the opposition bit the Local Board fo - the said district to a Bill now pending in Parliament, intituled "A Bill for incorporating and conferring powers upon the Widnes Brine Supply Com- pany, andfor other purposes." FRED H. GOSSAGE, Chairman of the said Local Board. Town Hall, Widnes, 10th Feb., 1890.

--- A " Times " telegram from St. Petersburg says that the recent fire in a house at Warsaw has revealed to the authorities the remains of no fewer th in seventy-six male ! children who have been made away with by the pro- prietress and some accomplices. DEATH OF LORD AUCKLAND. Lord Auckland died at Edenthorpe, Doncaster, on Thursday morning, at the age of 60. He had a paraly- tic seizure h few daye ago. Deceased, who was a Liberal in politics, is succeeded in the title by his eldest son, the Hon. William Morton Eden. MR. BIGGAR'S WILL. According to information supplied on authority to the "Freeman's Journal "on Thursday, the statement that Butlerstown Castle has been left by Mr. Biggar to Mr. Healey, M.P., is incorrect. The bulk of the property goes to his son, Mr. Joseph Biggar, but in the event of certain contingencies, the castle is left for the use of the ! local Roman Catholic Driest or priests.
